speakeroldname: Right Hon. L. S. St. Laurent (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am sure I can feel I am speaking for all members of this house when I say how deeply shocked all of us were to learn today of the sudden death of one whom all of us had come to regard as a personal friend, Mr. Karl Homuth, the member for Waterloo South. I am sure Mr. Homuth was one of the most popular of our members, and would himself like to be remembered, first of all, as a good companion and a warm personal friend of each one of us on both sides of the house.
When I saw him take part in the division in the house only last Thursday I hoped, as I know most of us hoped, that he was recovering his health which had been so seriously impaired in these last years. I feel that all of us, regardless of party, were of the opinion that the house would be better for having him once more in a position to take an active part in its proceedings.
I will not attempt any long or detailed review of the late Karl Homuth's public service. As hon. members know, he was elected to the Ontario legislature over thirty years ago, in the general election of 1919, and he was re-elected at several subsequent elections. From the time he was elected to this house at a by-election in 1938, until his death, he was successful on every occasion in retaining the confidence and support of the majority of the electors of his constituency.
No doubt a large measure of the support he was given was the result of the political allegiance of the electors in his constituency. But I am told, and I am sure no one here will find it difficult to believe, that a large measure of support came as a personal tribute from his friends and neighbours in Waterloo South.
I should like to express our sympathy to the leader of the opposition (Mr. Drew) on the loss of one of his senior supporters, and to ask you, Mr. Speaker, to extend the sympathy of all hon. members to Mrs. Homuth and her children.

speakeroldname: Mr. George A. Drew (Leader of ihe Opposition):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it was indeed a very great shock to all of us to learn this morning of Mr. Karl Homuth's very sudden
and wholly unexpected death. As the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) has so graciously said, he was a very warm friend of all the members of this house, regardless of their party affiliations. I think that few members here maintained their friendships on so broad a basis. For many long years he had been a figure well known here and well known throughout the country because of the vigorous views he had expressed, but views nevertheless expressed in such a way as to be accepted even by those against whom they were directed, in the generous and friendly spirit in which they were made.
Mr. Homuth was one of the many men who had served the public in a great many capacities; and over the broad field of public service that is open to every Canadian. As has been already pointed out, he was a member of this house continuously from 1938. Throughout those thirteen years he gave loyal and constant service to the people of the constituency which chose him. He also served for many years in the Ontario legislature. Prior to that he had served in the municipal council of Preston. His public service embraced the municipal, the provincial and the federal field. In each of those fields he was a good citizen in all that those words mean.
Many people are perhaps too often unaware of the extent of the service which is given by a good member to his constituency, and which is not in any way indicated by the contributions he may make to the debates in the House of Commons, or even to service on the committees. Karl Homuth played his full part in the debates of this house and in the work of the many committees. I think perhaps the members of the government know better than anybody else in this house that he was always an active representative of the people of his own constituency, no matter what their political affiliations were, in connection with every department of government where his services were required. That is a great and important part of the work of members of this house. I am sure that there were few members who were more successful in vigorously and correctly interpreting the needs of their own community than was the late Karl Homuth.
I join with the Prime Minister and, I am sure, with all the members of this house, in the expression of profound regret to his wife

The late Karl Homuth
and his family who have suffered this great and tragic loss. Karl Homuth will be remembered by everyone here as a good friend, a good Canadian and one who served his own community faithfully and well.

Mr. Speaker, twice during the last few days I have been reminded of some lines I read some years ago, that:
Death rides on every passing breeze.
He lurks in every flower.
On Friday we learned of the death of a distinguished civil servant in the person of Mr. Riddell. This morning we were equally shocked at the loss of one who has been here a long time, one who, as both the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) and the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Drew) have said, ably and well served his community and his country in this house and in representations before government departments.
Those of us who knew Karl Homuth in the old days, before his recent illnesses, remember him as a man full of vigour, whose witty interjections in this house often brought peals of laughter from all sides. He was never unkind; he was always friendly.
Those of us who have been associated with him for a long time, and even those who did not know him as well, today join the Prime Minister and the Leader of the Opposition, indeed all members of this house in regretting his passing and in expressing deepest sympathy to his widow, his immediate family and his brothers, who, I believe, have worked closely with him throughout the years.

Mr. Speaker, sudden deaths such as that of our late good friend Karl Homuth are always shocking. I am sure that a pall of gloom has settled over us all. Yet, sir, though he is considered to be dead, that is not my attitude at all. I do not look upon Karl as being dead. I look upon him as having gone away on a journey. But we shall miss him sorely, just the same, while he is away on that journey.
I have formed the habit of taking men as I have found them. I found that Karl was a good man. He was always good to me; he was always friendly and congenial. Often, as he passed down the corridor by the open door of my office, he would drop in with a word of greeting or to tell me the latest joke. On such occasions he was always pleasant and jovial. After he had left I invariably felt that the world was a better place because of men like him.
I know that Karl had been in indifferent if not poor health for the past several years or even more. We do not know just how long it was, because he never complained.

In all the time that I knew him I never once heard him complain. Only Friday last, when he returned to this house after a considerable absence, during which, I am told, he had a serious illness, he dropped in for a moment; and although he admitted that he was rather weak, he was still cheerful and uncomplaining.
I looked upon Karl as a warm friend, and I shall miss him in his long absence from us. My sympathies, Mr. Speaker, go out to his family in this hour of their sorrow, and to the Conservative party in the loss of a devoted and loyal supporter.
(Translation):

Mr. Speaker, I wish to say a few words in French to associate myself with those who have already expressed their sympathy on the occasion of the death of our friend, Mr. Karl Homuth. If, in this Holy Week, anyone should feel guilty for having prevented him from displaying his talents to the full during the last parliament, it is we of the "Little Chicago" group whose heckling I admit and regret. Fortunately, Mr. Karl Homuth was too broadminded and too much of a gentleman to hold that against us. If I have enjoyed the friendship of a member of the opposition like Karl Homuth, it is because he was big enough to put himself above anything we, without thinking of his illness, may have done to annoy him in the house. In fact, I was perhaps one of the first to shake his hand on his return to the house last Thursday.
I cannot express the regrets of the whole "Little Chicago" group, not being authorized to speak for the rest of its members. However, in view of Mr. Karl Homuth's attitude, I must say that I personally regret having said anything that may have offended a man who did so much good.
(Text):

Mr. Speaker, if I may be permitted to do so, I should like to make a request. It is known that Karl Homuth not long ago composed a prayer, or poem, in which he described life as a game, the bible as the book of rules, and God as the great Captain. I think it would be fitting if the leader of the opposition (Mr. Drew) could secure this prayer or poem and have it sent to us as a memorial. I make this plea because I was the first Liberal to meet Karl Homuth when he came upstairs; and I will not forget saying to him: "On behalf of the honest Liberals in the house, we bid you welcome." He said: "Thank you for the information." From that time we were warm friends.

Mr. Speaker, it is always a mournful sight to see the flag on the peace tower at halfmast. When one comes up the hill and sees the flag at half-mast the first question he asks is: For whom? Today I learned to my great surprise that Mr. Homuth had passed away. It was a great shock to me, although I knew that he had been ill. Last year he seemed to have recovered completely. I take this opportunity to add to the fine and well deserved tributes which have been paid to him.
We hear a lot about the fundamental freedoms, but there is no better example of the fundamental freedoms than this House of Commons. Members may hold diametrically opposite views, but when they depart this life their passing is lamented by the leaders and members of all groups in the house. We realize that in this house opinions are free, and the views of each member of parliament are respected by all.
I knew Mr. Homuth well enough to regret his passing, and I offer my deepest sympathy to the leader and other members of his party, his family, and his friends.

Mr. Speaker, as the member representing the riding of Waterloo North I wish at this time to pay a tribute to my dear departed friend, Mr. Karl Homuth. We did not think along the same political lines, but I think we were pretty much of one mind when it came to human values and friendships. Karl, as he was affectionately known to all of us in that part of the country, will be missed greatly. I wish at this time to add my tribute to those that have been paid to our late departed friend by the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent), the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Drew), and other hon. members.

Mr. Speaker, I cannot allow this opportunity to pass without having a word to say. Karl Homuth was one of my closest friends. He was a member of this house much longer than I have been. In the 1940 elections, when the Liberals won, leaving us only forty seats, Karl was my next door neighbour. He and I were the only ones left in that end of the province. Again in 1949, when there was another Liberal victory across the country, Karl and I were the only two left. I think perhaps he has been nearer to me than most.
He was a kindhearted man. I never knew him to hold spite against anyone. He had his own views, and he could express them before his first illness; but I think he held the respect of practically everyone on the other side of the house. I know that we are all going to miss him very much.

speechtext:
I rise
on a question of privilege. Your Honour will desire to know, I believe, that Canada, on the night of March 17, at Paris, France,
(Mr. Garson.]

retained the amateur hockey championship of the world, won for her last year by the Edmonton Mercurys of Alberta. The team which played for Canada this year was the Lethbridge Maple Leafs, also of Alberta, all Lethbridge boys, supported by Dinny Flanagan, Mickey Roth and Billy Flick, hailing from Stratford, Ontario. These latter boys, having played this season with the Kitchener-Waterloo team, were flown to Paris after their 1951 play-offs by the Canadian amateur hockey association, to help the Leafs win and to be on hand in case of injuries.
The names of the Lethbridge Maple Leafs are: Dick Gray, formerly of Medicine Hat, coach and defence player; Mallie Hughes; Carl Sorokoski; Don Vogan; Jim Malacko; Whitey Rimsted; Bill Gibson; Hector Negrello; Don MacLean; Stan Obodiak; Tom Wood; Bill Chandler; Lou Siray; Nap Milroy; Bert Knibbs.
Many of the players are married and the fathers of children. During their absence the salaries of the members of the team are being paid by the people of Lethbridge, who donated $10,000 in a drive to help make the trip a possibility.
Lethbridge invites all Canadians to be glad with her that reports convey that her boys, chosen and commissioned to represent Canada, have been: first, gentlemen on and off the ice; second, ambassadors of good will to all they met; third, a team genuinely great; fourth, an attraction of the first order, playing to over 250,000 people in their lengthy tour of Europe and frequently drawing crowds of 15,000 and more; fifth, an honour to their country in this additional respect, that in their tour they won the last 29 games. Then in the play-off they defeated Finland, 11-1; Norway, 8-0; Britain, 17-1; United States, 16-2; Switzerland, 5-1 and Sweden, 5-1.
This, I am told, is the thirteenth such title won for Canada since 1924. Will you join with me, Mr. Speaker, in congratulating Alberta, the fine young city of Lethbridge, and the Lethbridge Maple Leafs?

amount of items 62, 121, 204, 470, a sum not exceeding $4,040,634.67, being one-third of the amount of items 39, 456, 463, a sum not exceeding $536,759.17, being one-sixth of the amount of items 88, 566, 206, 209, 210, and a sum not exceeding $1,322,403.33, being one-twelfth of items 86 , 386, 395, 398 , 401, 411, 412, 415 , 417 , 420 , 451, 458 , 460, 495, of the said estimates, be granted to His Majesty on account of the fiscal year ending March 31, 1952.
He said: Mr. Chairman, the bill to be founded on this resolution is in exactly the same form as the bill we passed about this time last year.
It will provide one-sixth, that is to say two months, of all the items to be voted in the main estimates for the fiscal year 1951-52.
It will provide an additional three-quarters of four special items to provide for services on which the whole or greater part of the charges will come for payment within the first few months of the year.
It will provide an additional one-third of three special items to provide for services coming for payment within the first few months of the year but which do not require as great a proportion as the items to which I have just referred.
It will provide an additional one-sixth of five special items of which two are required to meet early in the year requirements of external affairs officers abroad, and three to cover the sessional expenses of the Senate and House of Commons, on which, as hon. members of the committee are aware, the heaviest charges come early in the year.
It will provide an additional one-twelfth of fourteen special items, mainly of a seasonal nature, connected with the experimental farms and so on, where heavier than normal proportions .are required to get activities under way in the early part of the year.
The general proportion of one-sixth for all services is intended to provide for all necessary ordinary requirements to the end of May. The additional proportions requested for certain special items, as I have indicated, are necessary because of the seasonal and sessional services affected, such as the sessional expenses of the Senate and the House of Commons, seasonal expenses of the Department of Resources and Development, early-in-the-year requirements of external affairs and trade of commerce for their offices abroad, and other services involving total commitments coming for payment in the first few months of the year.
In no instance is the total amount of any item being released. The form of the bill is exactly the same as the bill I introduced last year at about this time, and the several items are approximately the same as well. I give
Interim Supply
the usual undertaking that the passing of this bill will not prejudice the rights and privileges of hon. members to criticize and discuss any item in the estimates which will come up for consideration from time to time during the balance of the session.

In view of the statement that has been made by the Minister of Finance perhaps it is hardly necessary to add anything; but so there may be no doubt about it, approval of this motion does not imply acceptance of the contents of any of the items to which this resolution refers. It simply follows the established practice of making the necessary amount available to carry on the business of government until the accounts can be fully examined.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That is correct.

In the past it has been the practice of the government to give financial assistance in the marketing of feed grains across the country. Last year I believe about $18 million was spent for this purpose. I notice that in the regular estimates there is an amount of $4 million allotted, but there is nothing in the supplementaries. I should like to find out from the minister if it is the intention of the government to discontinue the feed grain subsidy, and if not, can he so assure the committee?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The estimates, Mr. Chairman, are in exactly the same form as they have been for several years past in so far as this item is concerned-freight assistance on western feed grain. It has been the practice to include in the main estimates an amount sufficient to pay this assistance until the end of the current crop year. The crop year, I understand ends about the end of July, and our fiscal year ends on March 31. We now have in last year's estimates an amount sufficient to carry it until the end of this month. The main estimates now before the committee provide for the continuance of feed grain assistance until July 31, the end of the crop year.
As has been the case in previous years, during the period between now and the time the main supplementaries are brought down, usually in June, the question as to the continuation of this assistance in the same or some other form will be considered. In past years, an amount sufficient to continue the freight assistance has been included in those supplementaries. As my hon. friend has pointed out, it amounts to between $18 million and $20 million to cover a full year. No consideration has yet been given as to what policy shall be followed with respect to the period after July 31. That will be brought, of course, before the house when the main

Interim Supply
supplementaries are tabled, late in May or early June. Does that answer my hon. friend's question?

No, not exactly. I did have unofficial assurance that it was not the intention of the government to discontinue the feed grain subsidy. There has been a lot of anxiety among farm organizations, in maritime organizations particularly, concerning not only feed grains but fertilizer which was also subsidized. In view of that anxiety, and certain statements that have been made in the press, can the minister not give the assurance that it is not the intention of the government to discontinue the feed grain subsidy? I would interpret his statement to mean that at least the present arrangement will carry on until the end of July, but that there has-been no decision whether it will be continued beyond that date. That sort of statement is likely to convince those who are anxious about the present arrangement that there is some doubt whether the feed grain subsidy is to be continued. It certainly leaves a doubt in the minds of those who may read that statement.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The situation is exactly the same as it has been in past years. The doubt may have arisen by reason of the fact that in this year's estimates, following a suggestion by the public accounts committee, a great deal more detailed information has been included. It is pointed out that the $4 million for this year is approximately the same as the amount in the estimates for last year, and it covers only the time up to the end of the current crop year. It is not customary to forecast government policy in advance of final decision.
I do not think I should add anything to the statement I made a moment ago. We are following the same practice as has been followed in prior estimates for several years. The reason why the small amount is included now is that the crop year overlaps the fiscal year.

I do not want to be out of order when the further supplementary estimates are before the house; consequently I am taking this opportunity of drawing the attention of the government, particularly of the Minister of Agriculture and the Minister of Finance, to a situation to which I referred just a year ago. In 1944 we appropriated $200 million for the support of agricultural prices other than wheat. This year I have again received, from the same person who wrote to me last year, a complaint about the lack of support for the potato growers of Prince Edward Island.
	Iff j
The minister will recall that last year I referred to a complaint from O'Leary railroad station in Prince Edward Island. Within the past few days the gentleman who wrote to me from there last year has written to me from Toronto. He says that he is in Toronto because the price received for his potatoes this year has been so low that he has had to move there to try to earn a little money to carry on his farming operations in Prince Edward Island. With his letter he enclosed his receipts for potatoes sold. I find that, between January 10 and February 22 of this year, the range of prices he received for his potatoes, before paying four cents a bushel for trucking, was 45 cents per bushel at the highest point and 40 cents per bushel at the lowest-that is for No. 1 Canadian table potatoes.
It seems to me that there is ground for complaint on the part of the potato growers of Prince Edward Island, and the other maritime provinces. I would draw attention to the fact that the appropriation which we thought was going to be used for the support of such agricultural prices has not been used to the extent that the house expected. As a matter of fact, in 1949, immediately before the general election, money from the agricultural price support appropriation was used, and that winter this man received an average of 69 cents a bushel. As 1 have said, within the last few months he received 40 to 45 cents per bushel, less the four cents for trucking, which brings it down to 36 and 41 cents respectively. I believe every hon. member will agree, without going closely into costs of production-and we know that they are not low for that type of produce in Prince Edward Island, because of the cost of fertilizer and so on-that those prices do not return to the producer a reasonable amount to enable him to live in the way we expect the producers of agricultural products to live in this country.
I am seizing this opportunity to bring this matter to the attention of the Minister of Agriculture, the Minister of Finance, indeed the government as a whole, to the end that some support may be given to these potato growers in the maritime provinces to enable them to continue to produce and to have a decent standard of living. After all, in the maritime provinces potatoes are an important agricultural product.

Mr. Chairman, I suggest that in addition to support the potato growers need protection. Today United States potatoes are being served in the parliamentary restaurant. These people are not getting any protection at all.

The question which has just been brought forward is one which has been under discussion continually throughout this season. Arrangements have been made from time to time which have been helpful, but have not brought a final solution of the problem involved. About a week ago the minister of agriculture of the province of New Brunswick telephoned me to know whether or not we would be willing to receive a delegation which would present to the government the problems of the maritime potato growers. That delegation is here today. I have been discussing potatoes all forenoon with this delegation from the maritime provinces.
Can you see eye to eye?

They are here this afternoon, as a matter of fact, meeting with a committee over in the agriculture department; and they are trying to work out some plan which may be of some assistance. I shall have a report, I expect, some time later in the day, or if not today, tomorrow morning, on the discussions which are now going on.
There are about 4,000 cars of potatoes unsold of this year's crop. That is not a quantity which is great as compared with other years. But the chief difficulty this year is that the potato price is very much lower in the United States than it was last year, or had been for some years previously, and when the double duty is applied at the end of the quota there is some doubt whether there is any market left in the United States for a considerable quantity of the potatoes, indeed probably for any of them. Under these circumstances it may be necessary to try to arrange some plan under which all the surplus can be converted into starch, or sold on the market in other parts of Canada as table potatoes. In any case, that is under consideration.
This condition has existed for some time. The house appropriated $200 million for support of such agricultural products, and apparently the support has not been given.

There was support given earlier in the year, but it was to assist in marketing the potatoes in Europe. These markets did not develop, for reasons which I shall be in a better position to discuss when we get to the appropriate item in the estimates.

I should like to draw to the attention of the minister the fact that the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar says that the price received by his friend on the island was 40 cents a bushel and 45 cents a bushel, less
Interim Supply
the trucking charge. The potato growers in New Brunswick sold potatoes as low as 25 cents a bushel, and some lower, less trucking charge, this fall, especially the veterans who had just taken up farming under the Veterans Land Act, and the young growers who have just started to farm.
The minister mentioned that there were
4.000	cars unsold. I believe there are 8,000 or 10,000 cars left in New Brunswick and Prince Edward Island. In New Brunswick there are six or seven thousand cars left, and I should like the minister to understand that. Every day now the banks and the machinery companies are seizing machinery from these potato growers, and the growers are leaving their farms by the dozens every week and going to Ontario to try to earn enough money to come back and pay their fertilizer bills so that they can carry on next year's farming operations.
I knew about the delegation being up here today. I hope that the minister will give them every encouragement, and that he will report to the house.

The minister referred to the delegation that is here and the conferences which are going on. If it is decided to give support in this instance, will the Nova Scotia growers be accorded the same consideration as that which may be accorded to the growers of the other two provinces?

That question of course will come up, as it always does immediately any decision is reached on the other areas. But I would just like to correct what the hon. member (Mr. Hatfield) said. I think when information is given out which is correct it is hardly proper for an hon. member to rise in his place in the house and say that it is not correct. I went all over this with the representatives from New Brunswick and Prince Edward Island this morning, and it is not correct to say that there are 8,000 or
10.000	carloads now unsold. There are
4.000	carloads unsold; the others are sold but not yet delivered. The position is that there are 4,000 for which there is yet to be a market found. I think it is much better to take the correct information rather than a statement that is not correct.
I have been in this business for the last forty-five years. I do not know where the minister got his figures, was it from the members of the marketing board? I do not think he got them from them.
That is exactly where I got them.

If I am any judge, there are
2.000	cars left in Prince Edward Island, and

Interim Supply
I am sure there are over 4,000 cars left in New Brunswick. After this time last year we had shipped over 3,600 cars to the United States; this year we are shipping very few cars there.

According to the latest
information, there are 2,000 cars in, each province not sold.

When this problem of potatoes is under consideration and the whole matter is being looked into, I hope the minister will not lose sight of the fact that the potato growers in the interior of British Columbia had a very difficult year last year, mainly on account of the early United States competition. I am not going to take the time at this moment to go into that, because I do not think this is the right time to discuss the whole question of protection, but I do hope when this matter is under consideration the minister will bear that in mind. I am sure they would rather have steps taken to ensure them a local market than be dependent on subsidies. The two problems are interrelated, and I hope they will be so regarded.

On the operation of that account, over the period referred to, there was a trading loss of some $8 million; but as against that, we earned some $50 million in interest accruals. This was taken up and explained in some detail, as I have mentioned, last year; and the insertion of this item in the estimates is to authorize the formal write-off of the trading loss in that account.

Will the minister just say a word about it? It was active and large over a period of years?

585. To provide, subject to the approval of the treasury board, for supplementing other votes for the payment of salaries, wages and other paylist charges-further amount required, $2,000,000.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: I take it this is the item that makes provision for the increases in civil service salaries which are to be made effective as from December 1, 1950?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That is correct. This is the balance of the amount we estimated we would need to pay arrears from December 1 to March 31.
Is the minister going to make a statement in regard to this?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I shall be happy to do so. The Prime Minister made a public statement on December 14, 1950, indicating the basis upon which it had been decided to give increases to the civil service. That statement indicated that it would be necessary to obtain a supplementary vote from parliament to cover them. I think I may have indicated previously that the cost of these increases for a full year will be something in the order of $30,000,000, so that for the four months of December, January, February and March something in the order of $9,000,000 will be paid out as supplementary payments.
There is a certain amount of money available to meet those payments in the votes of the various departments. In addition there is a certain amount left in the general salaries vote which, as the committee will recall, is the general vote available to provide for salary adjustments during the year. The information which we have received from the departments indicates that an additional amount of approximately $2,000,000 will be required in order to make the additional payment of some $9,000,000 representing the increases effective from December 1.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I certainly shall support this item and the proposal that our civil servants should get the increases which have been indicated. However, I should like to point out that civil servants are like other workers in this country in that the increases they get are all gone before they get them.

Supply-Finance
Before they are spent?

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
My hon. friend says, "Before they are spent." What I had in mind was the fact that the value of any increase is more than absorbed in the rising cost of living. The indication is that this increase is to be effective as from December 1, 1950. The last increase to civil servants was effective in October, 1948. During the period from October, 1948, to December 1, 1950, the cost of living rose by 11-5 points. Since the increase in civil servants' salaries and wages is put in terms of percentages it is only fair that I should translate that rise in the cost of living index from points to percentages. Therefore, I must say that the rise I have just referred to from October 1948 to December 1, 1950, was a rise of 7-2 per cent over the level as it stood in October 1948.
Before we get to the implementation of these increases we have had two further reports from the dominion bureau of statistics as to the cost of living index. The latest report is for February 1, 1951, at which time the over-all index stood at 175-2. That figure represents a rise in points from the last date of a civil service increase of 15-6 points. May I repeat that in terms of percentages? The cost of living has risen from October 1, 1948, the date of the last civil service increase, to the present time by 9-8 per cent over the October 1948 level.
I imagine that the minister will argue that the government is doing a fairly good job when they increase civil service salaries by what is reported to be an average of ten per cent. I understand that these increases vary from a low of four per cent to a high of 12-5 per cent.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The four per cent is in relation to the higher group. It starts at 10 per cent, goes up to 12J per cent and then drops rather sharply to four per cent.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
Correct, and the over-all
average is about 10 per cent. May I point out that by the time the civil servants get this 10 per cent increase in salary to take care of the 9-8 per cent rise in the cost of living we will have passed the date at which the cost of living had risen by that amount. I am prepared to make the prediction that today the cost of living index is already considerably higher than it was on February 1.
In addition to the increased cost of living faced by civil servants there has also been an increase in the number of hours per week that they work. If my arithmetic is correct that works out to an increase of 6-8 per cent. In other words, this increase in salary will just compensate for the increase in the cost

of living up to February 1, 1951. It will not compensate for the increased cost of living that has taken place since then, and for the further increases in the cost of living that are bound to take place before civil service increases are considered again. Further, it does not compensate for the increased work week which is the lot of the civil service.
I do not want to go into too many figures, but if you were to work out an index for the civil service and were to start with October, 1948, as 100 across the board and then take into consideration the rise in the cost of living and the increased hours per week that civil servants work you would find that the index of real hourly earnings for civil servants as at February 1, 1951, would be 93-8.
All of this it seems to me highlights the problem of our civil servants. I know the minister will say that it is the usual role of members of the opposition to approve of what the government has brought down and then say that it has not gone far enough, but I ask him to consider seriously the position of the civil servants. The government denies to them any effective collective bargaining rights. There are various civil service organizations, but collective bargaining as we know it under the provisions of the Industrial Relations and Disputes Investigation Act is not open to civil servants. It is also a matter of record that once an increase has been brought down there has to be a considerable period before another one is provided. It is a relatively short period this time if you take it from October 1, 1948, to December 1, 1950, but that period of two years and two months means that they can hardly look for a revision of this new scale until some time in 1953.
It seems to me that raises the whole question whether consideration should not be given to some sort of automatic cost of living bonus for our civil servants. That idea has already become quite current in contracts that trade unions are able to negotiate with their employers. That is particularly true in the United States where quite a number of employees work under an escalator clause which provides that whenever there is a certain increase in the cost of living index there is an automatic increase in the salaries or wages of those covered by that contract.
I have been trying to find out whether there are any recent examples of the same practice in Canada. I understand that recently, as reported on page 9 of the Montreal Gazette of March 12, 1951, the Robert Simpson Company approved of a plan whereby for its employees there is to be a 30 cents per point per week increase, in other

words $1.30 a month, as the cost of living index goes up. Similarly on page 5 of the Toronto Globe and Mail of March 6, 1951, it is reported that General Motors of Canada has agreed to a similar escalator clause. In this case the provision is for $5 per month for each 4-point rise in the cost of living index. I am interested in those figures because they seem to have a scientific basis. As I understand it, the cost of living index was worked out for the years 1935-39 on the basis of what was taken to be the average expenditure of a group of typical wage earning families surveyed in the middle of that period. The budget of this group, so I am told, was $1,453 per year.
That means therefore that a rise in the cost of living index of 1 point represents an increase of $14.53 a year in the retail prices of goods priced in the index budget. I may say when one takes that figure of $14.53 for one point, which is one hundredth of the total budget of the families who were surveyed, that no account is taken of the increased standards of living which we all accept as part of the progress that we are pursuing. I recall as a matter of fact a discussion with the minister's parliamentary assistant on that very point. He may have thought he was arguing with me, but the fact is that we both took the position that we do not want a return to the standard of living envisaged by the cost of living index basket of goods and services that was taken as the norm in the years 1935-39.
In other words what I am saying now is a case for arguing that a one point rise in the cost of living index should be considered as requiring more than $14.53 per year to meet that rise. Nevertheless I am prepared to take that figure as a minimum because it can be argued mathematically on the basis of the figures that were taken in arriving at the cost of living index. If a one point rise in the cost of living index means an increase of $14.53 a year in the prices of the goods and services covered by the cost of living index, that means that for any employee to be compensated for an increase of one index point he should receive an additional 28 cents per week or $1.21 per month.
I point out that the figures I have just given for the Robert Simpson Company and General Motors of Canada are reasonably close to the figure of $1.21 per month per point increase in the cost of living index. With regard to our civil servants my feeling is that they are not going to be greatly comforted with the increase they are now to get. They are counting on what they know has been announced by the government but as
Supply-Finance
they look into the future, realizing it will be two or three years before their salaries can be reviewed again, they face the prospect of the cost of living index continuing to go up with the result that their latter position will be worse than what it was before the increase became effective.
It seems to me that the only solution to this kind of situation is for the government to work out a plan similar to that in effect in the case of many collective agreements in industry whereby our civil servants would automatically receive an increase in their income as the cost of living index goes up. As a matter of fact I went to the trouble to ascertain figures as to what increases in the cost of living index would involve. For example, if the cost of living index reaches a figure of 180 the supplement on that basis would have to be $11.12 per month, over and above the present increase, on the basis of the rise in the cost of living as from December 1, 1950. If it reaches 185 it would have to be $17.37 per month. If it reaches 190 it would have to be $23.62 per month.
I submit with the way the cost of living index is rising that those figures are not unlikely at all. My guess is that when we come back after the Easter recess and have the figure for March 1 we will find' that it has gone up another two or three points above 175-2, perhaps to over 178, and that before the end of the year we will be up to a figure such as 190. If the minister says that my figures indicate that it would be a costly business for the government to consider an automatic increase in the salaries of civil servants, may I reply to him that those figures indicate the loss that the cost of living increase means to the civil servants themselves. Certainly it would cost the government $23.62 per month per employee to compensate for a cost of living index of 190. Similarly the average civil servant will be just that much short over his position as at December, 1950, namely, $23.62 a month, if the cost of living index goes up to that figure, and there is no compensation. I would be glad to hear from the minister as to what consideration has been given by the government to the position of civil servants from here on until the next time when their salaries might be subject to revision.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I do not know that I can add very much to what the Prime Minister said in the statement which he made outlining the proposed basis of increase to the civil service. In 1947 and 1948 the various civil service organizations urged upon the government the principle that salaries in the

Supply-Finance
public service should be directly related to the cost of living; in other words, that there should be an automatic increase with an increase in the cost of living index. As the committee will recall, that was tried during the war, and in the view of the government at any rate it had some very considerable defects. On both occasions to which I referred, in 1947 and 1948, the government decided not to accept that principle, mainly on the ground, I think, that it was not widely accepted in private employment, and because of the fact I think that we all recognized it would be very difficult to lower the bonus in the event of some decline in the cost of living. So on balance the government felt it was better to proceed on the principles I have outlined on several occasions, and which I think were reiterated by the Prime Minister in his statement to which I referred. As I have had occasion to say at other times, if the cost of living continued to climb of course the remuneration of civil servants would have to be adjusted, in the same way the remuneration of other groups in the community would have to be adjusted. Further than that I do not know that I would be prepared to elaborate at this time.

The hon. member who spoke a moment ago dealt very effectively, I thought, with the question of the cost of living in connection with those who are now inside the service. I wonder if I would be in order now to discuss the question of those who are without the civil service, who also are in very dire straits.

Item agreed to.
584. To authorize the write-off from non-active assets to the consolidated deficit account of the net trading loss in the securities investment account incurred between April, 1940, and November, 1949 ($8,299,183.77), $1.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I am sorry the hon. member for Greenwood has left the chamber; I now have the information he requested, which I might put on the record. I am sure it will meet his desire.

Between the fiscal years 1940-41 and 1949-50 the government of Canada purchased and sold its own securities pursuant to P.C. 10061 dated December 24, 1941. The purpose of these bond transactions was twofold; first, to profitably employ idle cash balances which the dominion had in the Bank of Canada and the chartered banks and which were not bearing interest; and secondly, to promote a better and sounder market for dominion securities during those years.
The face value of Dominion of Canada bonds purchased and sold during this period totalled $2,674,790,000. The cost of such securities was $2,715,145,837.34 and the proceeds from the sale thereof totalled $2,706,846,653.57, leaving a net trading loss of $8,299,183.77. Against this trading loss there was a total revenue from interest on the securities purchased of $53,067,559. This interest was taken into revenue each year as received and no portion thereof was used to reduce any possible losses on the principal amount involved in these bond transactions.
Last fiscal year, i.e., 1949-50, the amount of trading loss of $8,299,183.77 was written down in our books to non-active assets and accordingly constituted an expenditure charge in arriving at the budgetary surplus or decrease in net debt for the year. The purpose of this dollar item is merely to provide the necessary authority to write off this non-active account to the consolidated deficit account of Canada, which would have no effect on the budgetary surplus for 1950-51, nor on the net debt.

The other day in the public accounts committee it was brought out that securities totalling some $51 million had not been cashed by the public. I wonder if it would not be possible for the finance department to notify bondholders when a particular issue is going to be called, or when an issue is due. I say that because many people purchasing bonds today know nothing about such things. People have had bonds left to them, and they are just put away. We were told in the committee that one bond was taken and framed. So I wonder if it would not be possible for the department to notify these people that their bonds are being called or are maturing.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: As my hon. friend knows, the great majority of the bonds outstanding are bearer bonds, so there is no way of knowing who the holders may be. My recollection is that when bonds mature, and certainly if they are called ahead of maturity, the practice invariably is, as is required by the bond, to publish in various newspaper and other organs of public information-
But that is only in the financial journals.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No; when bonds are called we publish in the daily press. I know, because we have an item in the finance department appropriations to cover the cost of that advertising. In the case of the different series of victory loans we have been calling progressively for the last few years, notices have been published in the newspapers. As to the publication of a notice in connection with a bond which on its face falls due on March 1, 1951, whether we should remind the public of that by advertising in the newspapers, I shall be glad to consider. I must say I have always felt that in the interests of economy and the wise use of public funds we should not spend money to draw attention to the fact that people hold an obligation of the dominion which is coming due on a certain date. But we all know people are apt to be a bit careless about these things and not pay too much attention to the due date of a government bond, so possibly consideration should be given to a modest expenditure for that sort of thing.
The minister says he has no record in connection with bearer bonds, but the department must have some kind of record because when a person cashes a coupon at the bank he must sign a slip.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: We have no record at all. The income tax department may have some record of those who are cashing coupons; but the bearer bond, by its terms, means that it is a bearer security, and neither the finance department nor the bank of Canada has any idea who may be the owners of those bonds.
I am grateful for the statement given by the minister, which makes it clear that actually you did charge this amount as an expenditure in the year ending March 31, 1950.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I believe that is correct.

Therefore
you put yourself in the position of turning it into a non-active asset which you could write off, and you are now writing it off. The amount involved was very large, $2,715,145,837.34, and the minister has pointed out that this was done for two reasons, first to employ idle cash balances, and second to promote a better and sounder market for dominion securities during those years. Could the minister say what was the total amount in those votes at any one time? That would give us an idea how much of that $2,700 million is buying and selling.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I am afraid I could not, from memory. It was several hundred million dollars at one time, but it varied.

Item agreed to.
Supply-Finance
587. To provide for the transfer to the civil service superannuation account of a special government contribution of a portion of the amount by which the estimated liabilities exceed the balance in the account, $75,000,000.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I think perhaps I had better make a brief explanatory statement on this item, and give the house some background to this amount of $75 million which we are proposing as a special contribution to the superannuation account in order to provide for part of the deficiency which was accumulated in that account over a long period of years.
Under the Civil Service Superannuation Act, employees to whom the act applies contribute for current service at rates which range from 5 per cent to 6 per cent. In that regard may I say that male employees who were contributors prior to August 11, 1939, contribute 5 per cent. Other male employees in receipt of a salary of $1,200 or less contribute 5 per cent. Those in receipt of a salary of over $1,200 and not over $1,500 per annum contribute 51 per cent. Those in receipt of a salary of over $1,500 per annum contribute 6 per cent, while female employees contribute 5 per cent. Contributions may also be made for prior employment in the civil service, for some types of war service, and, under certain conditions, for prior pensionable service with a previous employer. The act does not require any specific contribution by the government but the practice has been to include annually an item in the estimates for a government contribution in an amount equal to the estimated current contributions of individuals in the previous fiscal year. In addition, interest at 4 per cent per annum is credited annually to the account, but no provision has been made heretofore for the matching by the government of past service contributions of employees.
The principal benefits under the act are calculated on the number of years of service, and the average salary for the last few years immediately preceding retirement. Contributions as provided for in the act with a matching contribution by the government will in general provide these benefits so long as the general level of salaries does not change appreciably. However, during the last decade or so there has been a substantial rise in the general salary level and future benefits under the act, being based on these higher salary levels, are thus greater than past contributions can provide.
I have been advised by the actuaries of the department of insurance that a substantial deficiency has accumulated, due principally to the rise in the general level of salaries and to the practice over the years of not crediting

Supply-Finance
the account with any government contribution for other than current service. An improvement in mortality among pensioners generally, and a tendency towards retirement at earlier ages, have also been factors contributing significantly to the deficit.
On the basis of an actuarial investigation made in the early thirties, there was a deficit of over $53 million in the account as of March 31, 1933. Two or three years ago we asked the actuaries of the department of insurance to undertake a further investigation and bring their earlier valuation up to date. While their report is not as yet in final shape, they advise me that the estimated accrued liability in respect of benefits under the superannuation act has continued to increase, and as of December 31, 1947, was in fact several times as large as the amount which we are providing for in this estimate. Hon. members will, of course, realize that what we are doing here is essentially to make a bookkeeping adjustment to reflect more accurately in our public accounts the magnitude of the liability to which the government of Canada is committed under this act. It is our hope that over the next few years it may be possible for us to make similar provisions for the remainder of the deficiency which has now been disclosed by the actuaries.
Although there is a substantial deficiency in the superannuation account, I think it is desirable to emphasize that it has arisen out of events of the past. While at a later date we propose to review the benefit and contribution provisions of the act with great care in the light of the detailed findings of the actuaries, present indications are that current contributions as provided in the act together with a matching contribution by the government will be probably about sufficient to cover benefits for employees entering the service in the future. If it should be found that the joint contributions of civil servants, and of the government as employer, are insufficient to cover the benefits provided by the act, we would hope to be able to suggest at this or the following session suitable amendments for the consideration of parliament.
I might also mention that the influences that have resulted in this deficit for which we are now making certain provision have not affected the civil service superannuation account alone, but have had a like influence on pension funds throughout the country. A great many other employers have had to make special contributions to their pension funds to offset similar deficits.

Can the minister state whether there is any difference
(Mr. Abbott.]
between "superannuation fund" and "superannuation account", two expressions he used?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No, they are the same. The superannuation account is the account we carry in the public accounts of Canada.

It would
seem, then, that contributions have about equalled payments out?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: There has been a small surplus of $2 million or $3 million a year in the last couple of years in the actual payments into the fund as against payments out. That is not particularly significant from an actuarial point of view, because of the fact that the number of people in the service has been growing and, as I indicated in my statement, rates of pay have been increasing.

Can the
minister give a little more detail about this vote of $75 million which his advisers have told him is needed?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
If my hon. friend will read
my statement in Hansard, I think he will find I have given a comprehensive statement of the principles involved in this vote. The actuaries are still working on an analysis of the fund. As he will appreciate, and other members who know about these matters will appreciate, it is an extremely complicated calculation which involves the question of mortality tables, the ages of the civil servants, the contributions which are being made, the rate of growth in the service, and so on. I indicated that in 1933 when a survey was made during Mr. Bennett's time, the indication was that there was an actuarial deficit of approximately $50 million.
A liability.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
My friend appreciates that
this is a charge against the government of Canada. There is a contractual obligation that when an employee has served so long in the public service, having made certain contributions, he receives a retiring allowance based upon that length of service and upon his average salary prior to the time of retirement. It is to reflect more accurately in our public accounts the ultimate liability of the taxpayers of Canada with respect to this superannuation that we are now suggesting that this transfer be made.

This $75
million will merely represent a book entry.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I said that in my statement,
that it is a book entry. We will credit the aocount with 4 per cent each year as earnings on the payment.
There will be another vote for that?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
That is statutory; that is
included each year.

Did I hear the minister state
it would be 4 per cent?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes, that is right, on the funds in the superannuation account. That is the rate at which interest is credited on that account, and that has been the case ever since the fund was set up, I believe.
Would it not be more realistic to take the rate which the government pays on annuities to the general public?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
It is certainly favourable
from the point of view of the civil servants, yes.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
I cannot but approve of
the action of the government in making good the bookkeeping deficiency which has been brought to their attention in connection with this matter. As the minister knows, there is another deficiency which I wish he would make good as well. He need not lounge back in his seat too far, as though I were going to make a long speech on this question. But I should like to remind him that the position of quite a group of our retired civil servants is still worsening.
On March 12 of this year, in response to a question of mine, sessional paper 102-C was tabled, bringing us up to date as to the number of retired civil servants that we have, and as to the amount of their pensions in various brackets. The total number of retired civil servants on pensions of one kind or another as at February 28 of this year was 9,877. In addition to that, there were 4,667 widows of pensioners drawing their share of the pension.
I find in this return, however, that of the 9.877 retired civil servants, 1,478 of them, or 15 per cent, are receiving pensions of less than $40 a month. That includes a group of 291 receiving pensions of less than $20 a month.
With respect to the widows, I find that out of 4,667 who are drawing their widows' pensions, being widows of retired civil servants, 2,647, or 57 per cent of them, are drawing pensions of less than $40 a month. That includes a group of 906 who are drawing pensions of less than $20 a month. I picked that particular figure of $40 a month because it is the old age pension figure; at least it is the maximum provided under federal legislation.
And as we know from the rising cost of living index, that figure of $40 a month today, in terms of 1935-39 dollar values, is worth less than $23 a month. I know all the arguments on the minister's side, as he knows
Supply-Finance
all the arguments on my side, because we have been throwing them back and forth for the last seven, eight or nine years. But it does seem that just as the minister now is bringing in an item of money to take care of something that arose out of a situation in the past, so he should face up to the problems of these people.
It has been pointed out that many of these people, whose case I argue, were people who v/ere working in the civil service during the early 1930's when there was a cut in their wages and salaries. Accordingly, the amount of the pension that they receive reflects the cut that they had to take at that time. But in the meantime-and the government has had something to do with it-the cost of living has gone up tremendously. I contend there is a moral obligation there that is equal to the contractual argument that the government uses, and that it is time that something was done to improve the position of those old, retired civil servants, particularly those in the lower brackets.
There were many above the $40 figure who would feel that their case should be argued as well, and so it should, but I make a special plea for those down in the very lowest brackets. The minister knows, because I have gone into it before, that some other governments do something about the position of their retired civil servants. I refer particularly to the three I mentioned on previous occasions, namely, the United Kingdom, Newfoundland and Saskatchewan; and I urge that further consideration be given to this matter.
I have had a great deal of correspondence with these people, as one might expect. Just a few days ago I was sent an exchange of correspondence between two retired civil servants one at The Pas, Manitoba, to a fellow retired civil servant in Winnipeg. They were discussing back and forth the situation, and the prospect for their future, and one asked the other what the situation might be if the new old age pension plan were to come into effect, and this was the reply:
I understand that we would come under that in addition to the pension that we are receiving now. According to reports, 19=2 may be when that would go into effect if passed. Unfortunately, a great number of us may be under the sod before then, or perhaps it might be fortunate for some of us if that happened.
That is not a nice way to put it, but it expresses the opinion of a great many of these people. They feel that, partly because their numbers are so small, they are literally being left out in the cold. I will not take more time on it now. I dare to hope that something might have got into the minister's

Supply-Finance
heart since the last time this was up, and that the matter might be reconsidered, namely, the matter of providing some cost of living bonus or other supplement for these people. I know the kind of letters I will get from them if nothing is done in the next little while-the minister will get them too-when they learn of the increase that we are providing for the civil servants, which I support. As a matter of fact, a few moments ago I was arguing that they should have a cost of living bonus as well. When they hear of this $75 million which is being provided to take care of the situation that flows out of the past they will wonder what it is that stands in the way of their getting an adjustment on their situation, their deficiency, which to them is very serious.

Mr. Chairman, it is not only a question of having a big heart. The minister has one, and everybody knows it. The hon. gentleman who has just spoken has said that the minister knows all about it. I know that he does. But I do not want him to forget one class of former civil servants, employees of the state. I mean the old employees of the Intercolonial Railway and the Prince Edward Island Railway and even the Temiscouata Railway. The former were civil servants inasmuch as the old Intercolonial was owned by the government before it was transferred to other companies with which it has been amalgamated. As the minister knows, the amount of superannuation of these employees is just a mere pittance, and I hope that the matter will be reconsidered by the government in due course. I know that the Prime Minister and all the members of the government are sympathetic to these people.
There is one thing that I want to say about the remarks made by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre. He has asked for bonuses without any discrimination between the civil servants. I presume it was that. Well, there should be a difference established between civil servants, the difference between those who are useful to the state and those who are not. There must be some means to establish the value of any civil servant to the state. It is not only a matter of commiseration and pity. I realize as well as the hon. gentleman that not only civil servants are affected by the rise in the cost of living index. It affects us all. I know. If you have one civil servant who does positively nothing and is surrounded by his staff, just as the sultan is surrounded by his harem, and surrounded by girls who do nothing except knitting, and by men who do nothing but chew gum and read the paper, then I do not see what increase that man
should have. We should see the efficiency and the usefulness to the state of each civil servant, and that seems only fair.
When they get into the service they think they are into a charitable organization, and then they have only to repeat their laments for an increase in salary. Members of parliament should have the courage to say that some civil servants are not worth their salt.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
We are talking now about
retired civil servants.

Some are retired, yes. I am speaking of those who will be retired afterwards and1 will enjoy the benefits of that legislation. I do not say that of all civil servants. There may be the exception, I do not know; but there are some civil servants who are completely dumb, who are not worth their salt, who refuse to work, who are procrastinators. They are good for nothing. They come here and ask for an increase in salary just the same as those who work and do well. There is something else that struck me forcibly the other day. I was listening to the radio and I heard the voice of a youngster who was speaking in a high-pitched voice to a gathering of civil servants. He said: Gentlemen, if you are not satisfied with the answer of the Minister of Finance, remember the railway strike, and we will tell the government what to do. That fellow should have been fired at once. There should be no strikes among civil servants. There is no reason for that. That is not the tone in which to speak. If they come to speak to the government, as the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre has said, submitting their grievances, I have no objection; but if they come on the warpath to tell the government: You must do this or we will strike; we will have a sympathy strike along with this group or that one, then I say they should not be received, and that the government should show a firm hand in dealing with them. Is the tail to run the head? We have seen that.
To the late prime minister I offered on a silver platter the control of the whole civil service, but he refused it at the time and it was lost forever-well, I hope not forever because I trust that the Prime Minister may be firm at the right moment, the Minister of Finance also, and all members of the government. As the supplementary estimates show clearly, they are ready to come to the assistance of civil servants who are worthy of consideration; but it is time to draw a distinction between those who are useful to the state and those who are not. I wonder how long it will take. They do not all deserve the same sympathy. There is a necessary distinction which must be made, and I hope that it will
[Mr. Knowles .1

be made in due course. I do not want the hon. member who has just spoken to say that I am not in sympathy with his suggestion. I am in sympathy with it, provided that those who get any benefit from it are those who are worthy of it.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: I am glad to have the sympathy and support of the hon. member for Temiscouata for my suggestion that something should be done to improve the lot of retired civil servants, particularly those in the lower brackets. Since he has indicated his agreement with the basic contention that I am making, I will not take the time to spell out my disagreement with a number of things that he has said. I should like to say this, however, on behalf of civil servants generally. I think that they accept-not only because it is in the law, but as a matter of principle -the denial to them of the use of the strike weapon. There is no question about that so far as civil servants are concerned. What they complain about is the feeling that at times advantage is taken of them because they have not the same effective bargaining power that is enjoyed by some other workers in this country. That was the point I was making.

If my hon. friend will pardon me, may I say that the other day I heard, with my own ears, over the radio, a man holding up the railway strike as an example, as a threat to the government, in order to get exactly what my hon. friend is advocating for them. I thought that was not the proper way to go about it. I hope that sort of thing will not occur again. That is all I want to say. But I was a witness to the lecture that was given on that occasion.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: I will not deny that, but-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I have only one comment I want to make on my hon. friend's remarks. I do not know what the civil servants feel and I do not know whether my hon. friend can speak with authority as to what they feel; but they certainly are not justified in feeling that the government takes advantage of the fact that they are not organized and do not exercise the strike weapon in order to fix unfair levels of salaries and wages. So far as my own experience goes, it has been that we have tried to lean over backward for that very reason. I do not think there is any justification for saying that the civil servants' salary scales are lower because of the fact that they, quite properly, have not the right to strike. I could not allow that sort of statement to go unchallenged.

Since the cost of living, from the time that controls
Supply-Finance
were first taken off, has risen about 60 points, has any consideration been given by the government to the giving of a cost of living bonus to these retired civil servants, especially those in the lower brackets to whom the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre referred?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: My hon. friend has been in the house only a short time. As the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre has said, I have dealt with this matter on numerous occasions. I do not know that I should attempt to reiterate what I then said, but briefly it is this. The right of the civil servant to superannuation is the same as any other contractual obligation. There are a great many people in this country who are not entitled to superannuation from anybody. They have to provide their own superannuation. There are a great many taxpayers in that position. I have never been able to see why one particular group who are paid out of taxpayers' money should receive preferential treatment. The people who have had to provide their own social security by small holdings of victory bonds and others who have had to provide their superannuation or its equivalent in other ways are not compensated out of public moneys for whatever increase there may have been in the cost of living. I am perhaps oversimplifying my argument, but the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre knows that I have elaborated it a great deal more on other occasions. In essence, that is the reason why the government feels that it is not justified in increasing this particular type of contractual obligation.
I have only one comment to make and that is that I do not agree with the position taken; I think it is unsound and unjust.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: As the minister says, we are both speaking in shorthand today, so far as our arguments are concerned. I simply want to make this reply to what he has said. These people are our employees, and I think that the government should be the model employer in this country.

Perhaps I should give a word of explanation of this item. In the further

Supply-Finance
supplementary estimates for the year now closing, the two votes referred to in this item were provided:

Is it possible to have a list of all those who have made claims, showing the amounts they have received from this government and from the provincial government, in connection with Cabano at least, if not for both places?

DEPARTMENT OF EXTERNAL AFFAIRS B-General-
580. The Canadian government's assessment for membership in the food and agriculture organization of the United Nations, further amount required. $109,000.
Can the minister give us a brief outline of the work being carried on by this organization?

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I think possibly the Minister of Agriculture would be-in a position to deal with this matter with more authority than I possess. As hon. members know, the food and agriculture organization is a specialized agency of the United Nations which deals with food and agricultural questions. Its membership consists of approximately 70 states, each with one vote in the conference or in the governing body which meets between conferences. The FAO is divided into technical divisions, of which I think there are seven. There are the divisions on agriculture, distribution, commerce, statistics, forestry and fisheries products, nutrition and rural welfare.
These divisions provide a wide range of fact-finding and advisory services designed to furnish information to the member states and to help them in the formulation of their agricultural policies. Canada has a real interest in the technical information obtained from

these various divisions. I believe the Department of Agriculture feels that useful services are being performed by them.
The FAO has been in existence for five years and during that period has established statistical services in the field of food, agriculture, forestry and fisheries which have been of use to our government and to the provincial agricultural services. The organization has also collected a great deal of technical information in these fields which has been made available to us and which has been of special assistance in the development of the agriculture of backward countries. If the hon. member would like to have more detailed information I can secure for him a copy of the report of FAO which deals with these matters at much greater length.

Is not most of this money being spent to send agricultural representatives behind the iron curtain to teach the people there how to farm with tractors and agricultural machinery bought with Marshall aid funds in order that the products may be shipped back to this country or to the United States?

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I am not sure that I quite gather the import of my hon. friend's question. I would point out that there are no countries behind the iron curtain which are members of the food and agriculture organization. They have all withdrawn from that organization and are not now receiving any assistance from it.

They were receiving assistance. I was at the United Nations at Lake Success and we heard a man who had just come back from the Ukraine where he said he had been trying to show the farmers how to use tractors, gang plows and other agricultural machinery that had been shipped under the Marshall plan. Before that time they were using only wooden sticks for plows. speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, at the last session of the general assembly a resolution was passed providing for a program of relief and rehabilitation for Korea where of course the need is very great and getting greater every day. A committee of the assembly discussed this matter at great length and a United Nations commission for relief and rehabilitation of Korea was set up. That organization drew up a plan of action and reported back to the United Nations. Its plan was also very carefully considered by the economic and social council. It is estimated that about $250 million will be required to meet the immediate needs. That of course will not begin to cover the whole problem of rehabilitation.

This was some weeks ago. Of course there has been more damage done since that time, and there have been more refugees moving south. We felt that as a government we might ask parliament to agree to appropriate an amount which would be roughly proportionate to our share of the United Nations budget. The director general of the organization is Mr. Kingsley, who has been director general of the international refugee organization.
