We are now rebuilding what we have destroyed. The temple of Jerusalem was destroyed and it was hard to rebuild it in three days. The destruction has taken place, and what surprises me is the amount of the contribution of the United States, the United Kingdom and Canada. I wonder if the amounts for rehabilitation are in proportion to the loss and damage caused to Korea by each of those countries. Naturally no one knows about that. United States bombers were there. They were very active and caused more damage than the Canadian destroyers or the few Canadian soldiers who have been there. That is evident.
I should also like to know how the United Nations came to establish Canada's share for the rehabilitation program in Korea at $7,250,000. What is the use of destruction when we have to rebuild afterwards? I know that life is perpetually recommencing. On the other hand, a country is destroyed and then we proceed to rebuild it again. Coventry is not yet rebuilt in its entirety. In many parts of Europe there are still ruins dating from the last conflict, and no new buildings have been erected there. I find it very sad. I am not a pessimist but we hear of war every time that there is a sitting of

the house. It is war, war, war. Now we are trying to rebuild what has been destroyed. Would it not have been easier not to destroy and therefore not have to rebuild?
That is a suggestion that may arouse the minds of some of my colleagues but I find that the war in Korea is very pitiful. I was the only one to say that in the house last June, and some hon. members gave me the cold shoulder at the time. What progress has been made in Korea up to now? The armies go up to the 38th parallel and they come down. Now they are nearing the 38th parallel and the newspapers are full of news of a possible total war. How can we rehabilitate Korea if we have a total war? There are some Canadians in Korea in the Canadian army. For a time they complained that they were not dressed warmly enough. I have every sympathy with the Korean people. It is not because they live in the antipodes that we have the right to be indifferent to their sufferings. As human beings they are entitled to our consideration and the consideration of the whole world. No country has publicized the tragedy and misery of Korea to such an extent as the United States, through the big magazines of that country which have published illustrations showing refugees wandering about in numbers, without shelter, deprived of food.
I ask the minister a supplementary question, which he may answer whenever he feels like it. If we vote this amount of $7,250,000 for the rehabilitation of Korea, can we be sure that our men there who may be wounded, and the Koreans themselves, will get some advantage from it? I hope so.

speechtext: I will try to get the information the hon. gentleman has requested in regard to these other agencies. speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, this item covers the cost of replacing two schools that had been in operation there for a number of years, and which were destroyed in the the conflagration that occurred at Rimouski last spring. Arrangements were made with the provincial government that there would be a contribution of 50 per cent towards the damages suffered by a number of individuals, and in addition to that the federal government and provincial government would contribute on a 50 per cent basis to the rebuilding of these two schools which had been erected originally as a consequence of joint contributions made by these two governments.
Will the minister state whether there is any insurance on buildings of this kind held by the government?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
There was insurance, and it was applied to the rebuilding, but the insurance was quite insufficient. The cost of the equipment is much more than the amount of the insurance. Originally the equipment for the marine school had been provided from war assets out of the "innards" of one of the corvettes. The insurance was for a sum much below the market value of equipment of that character when new. It cost more than the amount that was provided by the insurance to instal the kind of equipment required for this training.
When this matter arose I was concerned. I had been down there at the time of the fire, and I knew something of the situation. When these accounts were submitted, I found that they were high, and though the commission originally did not have any jurisdiction in respect of government property or property that had been contributed to jointly by the two governments, we asked that the commission check all the items to make sure whether or not proper care had been taken in the restoring of the schools. As a matter of fact the people down there had gone ahead with the work, making their own arrangements. There was a corporation administering this marine school, and they had gone ahead on their own because they wanted it re-established as rapidly as possible. We had agreed that we would contribute 50 per cent of the cost of the contract provided it was let to the lowest tenderer. As a matter of fact, when that arrangement was made the thing was already more than two-thirds completed. In order to be sure that it had been carefully handled, we asked

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: The committee was considering item 595, in the Department of Labour. Shall the item carry?

Mr. Chairman, this is an item to authorize and provide for federal contributions to reimburse the province of Quebec for one-half the expenditure for the reconstruction of buildings of technical and marine schools at Rimouski, Quebec, and one-half the cost of re-equipping the technical school, and to authorize the Minister of Labour to enter into an agreement with the province of Quebec for such expenditures.
May I say first of all that this item has my hearty support. I presume these unfortunate people lost their schools through the fire, and they are now being helped by the federal government to restore those educational facilities.

It is a worthy cause, and I hope the government has made the grant sufficiently large.
However while supporting this expenditure I would point out that this is a grant in aid to education in Quebec. It is a grant from the dominion government to a province, and earmarked as an expenditure for education. The last three words in the item, "for such expenditures", are reminiscent of the last few words of the resolution I moved on February 22 of this year. Those words were, "by the granting of financial assistance to the various provinces for that purpose." I see my genial friend, the Minister of National Health and Welfare, in his seat, and I would recall to his mind that it was on those words that he based his special and final argument.
Here is a dominion grant for an expenditure on education, such expenditure to be given to a province. We have every sympathy in the world for this town which suffered so disastrously from fire, and we are pleased to see that they are being given this assistance. However I would point out that while this is a special case-and this is what I rose to say-a district such as the town of Rimouski which was prosperous enough to afford that type of school on its own account, but which lost it through fire, is in no worse plight than many corresponding districts which have never been able to afford that type of school, simply because of a lack of ability to pay for it.
I hope the people of Quebec will not feel that this grant is interfering in any way with their autonomy in matters of provincial education, or that that autonomy has been violated by the giving of this grant, or that dominion-provincial relations will be impaired thereby. I presume this grant is being given without suggestion of any control whatsoever by the dominion government, except that it be spent for the purposes indicated in the vote. I am sure someone will disagree with me before long when I say that this is just another precedent in a long list of precedents of grants earmarked for purposes of education, and which have been granted by the federal government to a province.

Mr. Chairman, all hon. members appreciate the full explanation given by the Prime Minister with respect to this grant. I am wondering however, as did the hon. member who has just taken his seat, if we are now setting a precedent, and whether we may look forward to its being extended over a wider area so that it will not be confined alone to the province of Quebec; or is it a precedent which in future the government may regret? If we are going to base our grants on needs and expectations- and I refer in passing to the $65 million grant

-there will be many municipalities in Canada that will be hoping to come under the same provision or to receive the same help from the federal treasury.
Some time ago I mentioned that the burden of taxation on real estate was becoming very heavy, and that I hoped the federal government would see its way clear to give grants in aid of education to a degree greater than has been done in the past. I have been wondering how many students were going to the school in question, and how great an area it serves.

Mr. Chairman, I am not able to answer the last question, but I shall try to get the information for my hon. friend. Referring to the comment made by both hon. members, however, they both know that in their respective provinces, as in all provinces of Canada, a federal-provincial program has been under way in the field of vocational and technical training. This operates on a two-way basis: on the one hand by way of assistance in capital expenditures, which would correspond with the present instance- and consequently this does not set a new precedent-and, on the other hand, assistance to vocational training students.
When the main estimates are before the committee I shall be able to give a full report in this matter as it affects all provinces, and at that time I shall endeavour to have details with regard to this particular school.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I have a figure here which indicates that 342 students had been enrolled up to October. I understand that a considerable number have been refused because they were being housed in what formerly had been a shed, and such facilities could not be made sufficient to care for any more than the 342.
This happened to be a school; but it was a part of the aid extended in the province of Quebec because of the disaster that had occurred. That aid was extended, not particularly in respect of schools, but as a part of the general aid extended following the precedent that had been established in connection with the Fraser valley floods, and then the Red river floods, as a consequence of a disaster that, rightly or wrongly, was regarded as being too extensive to be left to the resources of the locality.
It happened to be a school; but it was because of the nature of the disaster-and in that respect I am sure the hon. member hopes, as I do, that it is a precedent of disaster that will not occur very often elsewhere.

I must thank the Prime Minister for what he has said. But I will say to

Where there is a will there is a way, as this item so well demonstrates.

Mr. Chairman, this is the second attempt today I have made to speak about a matter which I think is of extreme importance to all members of this house. I shall start off by complimenting the government, and particularly the Minister of Labour, upon the work they are doing with respect to the screening of the film "Date of Birth." The pamphlet which has gone out with respect to that film I believe has done a tremendous amount of good for a great number of people in Canada. It is of that particular group that this film was designed to assist that I wish to speak tonight.
There has been a tendency to refer to men and women in industry and unfortunately in the civil service as being too old at forty-five years. I think that argument is completely and utterly erroneous and in order to indicate what happens when we consider a cross-section of Canada, I have tabulated, not to the nth degree, what would happen to the membership of this House of Commons if everyone over forty-five years was ruled out of court. It was rather startling to me when I went through the red bible of the parliamentarians to find that if we removed those who are forty-five years or over from the house with a membership of 262, we would have only 66 members, and among those would be just two cabinet ministers. It might be that such a housecleaning would expedite the business of the house, but I rather doubt it. If the numerical strength of the house were decreased, the quality generally of the house would be decreased.
I give those figures simply to illustrate the over-all picture in the Dominion of Canada. I intend to deal only with the age group of 45 to 69. I find that there are 1,431,000 males in that group and 1,312,000 females, or a total of 2,743,000, or roughly 20 per cent of our total population. I have taken those figures from the Canada Year Book of 1950 and they are applicable to the end of 1948.
Coming now to what the Department of Labour is endeavouring to do with respect to this age group, I commend for hon. members' consideration a pamphlet which has been put out by the Department of Labour over the signature of the deputy minister entitled, "A progress report on 'Date of Birth' ". In that pamphlet we find some helpful information. It brings us up to January 15, and on page two there are certain

comments which I should like to draw to the attention of the committee as follows:
The film was designed to bring to the attention of the Canadian public, and community and national leaders in particular, the problem of the older worker in obtaining employment with a view to expanding employment opportunities for these workers.
We find that this film has been shown in Canada 751 times, and that it had a total audience of approximately 58,000. Here are some of the comments after the film had been seen by various executives and businessmen across the length and breadth of our land. On the same page paragraph (b) reads:
In an Alberta city the personnel manager of a large department store telephoned the local office to state that as a direct result of seeing the film this firm was placing an order for five older people to train as sales clerks.
Paragraph (c) reads:
. . . the sales manager of a large firm reported he was hiring thirty salesmen in western Canada. After seeing the film he decided to insert in his advertisement "that age is no barrier." This advertisement was to appear in all western newspapers.
Paragraph (d) on the same page reads:
After a showing of the film to the personnel managers' association the personnel director of one department store reported that he had revised the age radius in several occupations in their store to include workers from forty-five upwards in their hiring program.
On page 4 we also find some very revealing information. Toward the bottom of the page, with reference to the Ontario region there is the following:
I unhesitatingly believe that this film has done an outstanding job in placing before the proper persons the problem of the older worker with a lasting effect, and in many cases direct results.
There have been beneficial and practical results. In addition there is the following:
For example, there is no doubt that the twenty-eight showings of the film in the Toronto area have developed an impetus in opportunities for senior citizens. Many individual orders have resulted from this publicity. As a result of one showing six orders were received in the local office for older workers.
I think that this is one of the very important bits of work that the present government is carrying on to a degree of great fruition. We are short of many skilled labourers in the Dominion of Canada. We also have many semi-retired people who actually are not desirous of attaining full retirement and have not at the present time . a sufficient bank roll to maintain themselves. They have a great desire to work if and when work is provided for them to do. Many authorities have been quoted in this house, all of whom I presume are in the nature of things much greater authorities than I, but I should like to quote what I stated with

respect to this problem on a radio broadcast to the Vancouver area on March 6. At that time I said:
It seems to me there is one particular class in the Canadian community that must now be afforded some additional protection against the high cost of living. That is the great community of people across Canada who are on fixed incomes. It matters not whether those fixed incomes are old age pensions, annuities, disability pensions, veterans allowances, or retired pensioners from industry and the civil service. It seems to me that these groups are the ones who should have greatest consideration immediately by measures which will alleviate their present situation. I think it is also fair to say that the time is now opportune for the government and parliament to consider the question of men and women who are considered too old at forty-five . . . I am sure we are all agreed that forty-five years of age does not mean that a man's or woman's capacity to produce is over, and with such a great amount of manpower being required in our defence efforts this is the logical time for parliament to consider giving a better deal than now exists for those in this age category.
There are revealing figures in the Canada Year Book with respect to this problem. I think it was Horace Greeley who at one time said:	Go west, young man, and grow up
with the country. I might reiterate that when you look over the list of figures compiled in the Canada Year Book you find that there is a surplus of men in Canada in all age categories from forty-five up to seventy-five. But apparently when one reaches the three-quarter century mark in one's travails through this mundane sphere the old man of the family sloughs off through hard work in order that his wife may have some of the better things of life to think about after he has gone.
At seventy-five we see there is a complete balance of 85,000 males and 85,000 females. The ratio from then on up to 90 plus is all in favour of the widow or spinster. I am informed that there is a great plethora of females in the city of Ottawa, and so I say that what the girls should do is go west and grow up with the country. In the riding of Cariboo in the northern part of British Columbia-my hon. friend behind me nods his head-it has practically become a matter of notable history in Prince George that no girls who go into that country as nurses and school teachers have ever lasted in single blessedness for more than eighteen months.
To me there is a great urgency with respect to this problem. This afternoon one hon. member raised the point about securing a higher standard of living for our civil servants. I am all for that but, Mr. Chairman and hon. members, I want to make a plea to you that we do something now, not next year or the year after, for men and women who are forty-five and cannot get into the civil
Supply-Labour
service. It seems to me a great many of those people are living on fixed incomes on a pension basis which have long since lost their purchasing power in the markets of this country. So I am very much in sympathy with doing something now to better the living conditions of those men and women on fixed incomes. As I have stated, only 66 persons in this house are under the age of 45, so I think it must be recognized that people over that age make a tremendous contribution to the biggest business in Canada, the business of governing the country. On the same basis, Mr. Chairman, I say those people have a great contribution to make whether within or without the civil service, provided the government will give them the opportunity to do so.
In thinking of this great question I tried to find out something about a gentleman who a few years ago started a business in one of the larger metropolitan centres of Canada. This man was disabled in the first war. When the second war broke out things were not too good, and he determined to start a business where the first consideration in hiring personnel would be that men or women should be selected who were 45 or over, either fit or suffering some disability from one cause or another. He found by actual comparison with conditions in a similar industry in another city that he was getting much less absenteeism from those employees of mature age who were to some extent physically handicapped. He also found that while a group of younger personnel might do a certain task quicker, over the long haul the older workers, men or women, disabled or otherwise, gave more continuous, active and efficient service.
Having that in mind I think we as members of parliament should give all possible assistance to the work outlined in this pamphlet, "Date of Birth", because this is the sort of liaison between employer and employee that industry throughout Canada needs today more than ever before, when in many categories of labour we are actually scraping the bottom of the barrel. Surely working together we can evolve some scheme to assist these people who will find themselves in dire straits unless they are able to secure employment.
I appreciate that people over this age have not been able to get into the civil service because of pension qualifications. Well, we have some excellent actuaries employed by the government, and I believe a way could be found to open the door to employment in the civil service for these people of 45 or over, who are so much steadier than people of 25. Surely we can find a way of making their employment possible, just as the provincial

Supply-Labour
government took steps to aid in the employment of disabled persons who returned from overseas after the last war. Arrangements were made in factories under provincial supervision whereby certain percentages of their time off through illness or accident were paid for by the employers as well as by the employees under the Workmen's Compensation Act.
I believe we should give this matter very serious and earnest consideration, because in this category of men and women across Canada I think we have a most stable influence in our whole national economy. It is not good enough for any government at any level to say these people on meagre pensions, regardless of the source of those pensions, have contributed to what they are now receiving and it is simply unfortunate that the purchasing power of the dollar now is not what it was when they were pensioned off. I join heartily in what was said today by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre about those in the civil service, only in reverse. I am expressing the same sentiments, I trust, when I say I am for those who are outside the civil service. I am anxious that they should get consideration equal to that given those in the service, and I believe a way can be found to do that.
I am going to conclude by suggesting to the government with all the force at my command that we come to grips with this problem, not next year or the year after but now. We should avail ourselves of the services of this group of men and women who do not desire charity but who are determined now as always to make their own way in life. Their only desire is to be of service to Canada, either their native or their adopted land. So, sir, in all sincerity I ask the most serious consideration of this problem by the government, so that before many days or weeks, we may come up with an answer that will give us individually and collectively a great lift because we will have done something for Canada. If it is good for Canada it is good for them and good for us. Vive le Canada! God save the King!

I agree with the hon. member who has just taken his seat, that this age limit that is placed against people forty-five years of age and over by both the civil service and industry of this country should not exist. As the hon. gentleman has pointed out, the reason industries say they cannot take these people into service is that they cannot make their pension plans actuarily sound. It is not on this particular matter that I wanted to say a few words this evening. We have a very serious situation in the coal mining town of Inverness. The

principal coal operation there is carried on by the government of Nova Scotia. It has been losing between $350,000 and $400,000 a year. Today there is a motion before the provincial legislature to have the government close down this mine. I may say that the members who are proposing it are not Conservative or C.C.F., but are supporters of the Liberal government of Nova Scotia.
Strange to say the man who is doing most of the objecting to the continuance of this operation comes to Ottawa about four or five times a year in order to get $125,000 to help a concern in the northern part of Cape Breton county get their products to market by giving them deeper dredging. I have supported that, too, but it does seem to me to be a dangerous precedent for the gentleman from Halifax who has made this motion. However, that is by the way.
I am in hopes, Mr. Chairman, that this mine will not be closed down this year. I should like to bring to the attention of the Department of Labour the fact that if this mine is closed down all those miners who are over forty-five years of age and out of employment will find it difficult to get work. The chief employer of miners in that area is the Dominion Coal Company and, rightly or wrongly, they do not employ people who are over forty-five years of age. There are a few other small coal operations around Inverness county, but they are well manned now. I am fearful of what is going to happen to those miners, roughly between 300 and 400, and their families if this mine should be closed this year or in the near future.
I am bringing this to the attention of the Minister of Labour in the hope that something can be done to assist those coal miners by way of unemployment insurance if this disaster should come about. Last year something very helpful to many people in my constituency was done, and that was the supplementary aid in connection with unemployment insurance. I know of eight or ten persons, not fishermen but people who were doing different work, who did not get the required number of days' works to qualify. The Department of Labour, through this unemployment insurance commission, did come to their aid when the matter was brought to their attention. Mr. Chairman, I do not know whether it is possible to do something about a situation such as this, but I am bringing it to the attention of the minister because I am fearful of what will happen in that time.

I want to express my gratitude to the member for Yancouver-Burrard for his encouraging words. I am sure that they

will, in truth, be encouraging to the officials of the national employment service, who come under the Minister of Labour, and also those who are also working to assist in the employment of older veterans, who come under my colleague the Minister of Veterans Affairs. The hon. member has brought forward a very important question. It is true that the employers of labour are increasingly sympathetic and receptive to the idea of employing older people. Owing to the depression of the thirties, the gospel was then preached that we should get people out of employment somewhere around sixty to make jobs for those coming along. Now we should, from two points of view, reverse our steps. First, from the point of view that those who want to work should have an opportunity to work, and also because of the need for greater production.
The film to which the hon. member referred has been well accepted across the country. While my officials have co-operated in its preparation, the fulsome compliments I have to divert to the national film board under the direction of my seatmate the Minister of Resources and Development. To the imagination and ability of the people on the film board who are responsible for producing this film goes most of the credit.
In speaking of the older workers may I say that they have, in fact, been incapacitated for work because they have not been given the opportunity to get jobs. We are trying our best to overcome that. These people are thus associated with another group namely those who are incapacitated for work because of some physical disability, and the reluctance on the part of industry in offering them jobs as compared with fit men and women. As for the second group, I am hoping that before too long my colleagues the Minister of National Health and Welfare and the Minister of Veterans Affairs will have an opportunity of telling the house some of the plans that were evolved during the federal-provincial conference at Toronto attended by the three of us early in February. At that time the important voluntary agencies, all provincial government departments affected, and all three federal government departments affected, were represented, and they worked out recommendations which I believe will be useful in helping to solve the problem of those incapacitated owing to physical defects. I can assure the member for Vancouver-Burrard that this whole problem is receiving the full consideration of the government, of my department, of the unemployment insurance commission and of the national employment service. These organizations are now
Supply-Labour
actively engaged in efforts for the improvement of the lot of the older and incapacitated workers.
In so far as the request made by the member for Inverness-Richmond is concerned, I shall be glad to look into that situation and see what we can do.

Mr. Chairman, I just have a few observations to make on this item. At this stage of the session when the supplementary estimates are before us, I know it is not the proper time to make an extended speech. I should like to support the statement made by the member for Inverness-Richmond. That particular town has taken a bad beating for the past twenty years. It is a mining operation that was destroyed by faulty development under free enterprise. When it was no longer profitable it was taken over by the provincial government, and has been operating for the last twenty years more or less as a relief project.
Like many other industries in our economy, it is necessary but not self-supporting. That industry has been subsidized and operated by the provincial government over the years because it provides the means of a livelihood in that particular area, and is necessary to the economy of a large section of Cape Breton Island.
I have commended the provincial government for doing it. They pay wage rates prevailing in the rest of the industry, but because of the shrinkage of that particular operation over the past couple of years men have been laid off periodically. They have no chance of employment elsewhere because, as the hon. member for Inverness-Richmond pointed out, they have reached the age when organizations like the Dominion Coal and Steel Company will not take them on, and they are permanently unemployed, despite the fact that they are still productive.
There is a threat of closing the mine; and, as the hon. member has suggested, it will throw out of employment perhaps 300 men who have families, and who have a stake in the community. A town has been built around that industry. There is a big investment there on the part of the community. There are schools and churches, and that has to be taken into consideration.
My main objective in rising was to ask the Minister of Labour whether any thought has been given to the possibility of extending the unemployment insurance benefits, I do not say right across the country, but in areas such as the one referred to, which is affected in the manner indicated. A man becoming unemployed in that particular area, with a family on his hands, is through. There is not much chance of his getting out, and most

Supply-Labour
of them are over the employable age, because it is the national policy of every industry in Canada, and has been since 1945, not to employ a person over 40 years of age, and they are sticking to that policy.
With his officials the minister might consider the possibility of extending unemployment insurance in an area such as the one I describe until such time as more gainful employment can be found for these people either in that community or elsewhere, because if we can take 600 Germans to northern Ontario, pay transportation and train them in the metal industry of northern Ontario, then we certainly have a similar obligation to Canadian citizens who have been paying taxes over the years. That is not an unreasonable request. I would ask the minister to take a look at that particular subject.
My second point is this. Over the years there has been a demand to take in the fishing industry. There are hundreds of fishermen who are employed probably eight months or nine months of the year, but there is a period when they are out of employment. I do not think you would be adding any additional burden to the Unemployment Insurance Act if the fishing industry were taken in, because they are totally unemployed for only a couple of months of the year. The contribution you would get from that industry would offset any expenditures you may have to make during the seasons when certain types of fishermen are unemployed. I bring that again to the attention of the minister so that his actuaries may have a look at it and ascertain if it is not possible to. bring them under the act. But I want him definitely to be able to make an answer to the house before it closes next June or July on this particular program of extending the benefits of unemployment insurance to areas such as Inverness, and to other places where unemployment is a permanent thing, where, because of the present industrial policy right across the country, people over 40 years of age are not going to be employed any more. They are too young for pensions. There is no picture into which they can fit.
Another thing I want to mention to the minister is this. Anyone who says that industry is co-operating a hundred per cent with the employment offices does not know very much about it because it is not. In practically every industry that I know of employment offices have been set up. These industries have their own employment agents, and they by-pass completely the unemployment insurance offices which have a tabulation of all the unemployed in the area. Those offices know what these unemployed

people are fitted for, how long they are unemployed and what their family obligations are, and the unemployment insurance offices are in a position to give proper direction in every community across this country to the employers, if the employers will make their needs known to them and take direction from the offices, instead of setting up their own employment offices. In that respect they are not co-operating. They by-pass them.
But more than that, contracts are let by the government in many communities across this country. They are federal contracts. When the contractor comes in, instead of going to the employment offices and getting his men through those offices, he will accept slips from people all over the community, from local politicians of all kinds. I have been on jobs, and I have seen the type of personnel that a contractor had to take because of that vicious patronage system. His work was hampered, he told me, because he did not get the right type of man. He knew that if he had the right to go to the employment office, and if the employment officer could direct personnel to him, he would have obtained the kind of people he wanted.
I said I was not going to take very long. I hope the minister will take a look at tonight's Hansard before the end of the session and see if he cannot correct these few sore spots in the act.

It is fortunate that the
Minister of Labour follows the footsteps of his predecessor, the late Mr. Mitchell. He is sincere and friendly and that is why he so often meets with success.
Unemployment insurance is a big organization, and the personnel is working in a satisfactory manner. I have just a question to ask the minister. I am sure he is not in a position to answer now but I hope he will be kind enough to convey the information when he gets it. I should like to know the number of people who have received unemployment insurance during the last twelve months in each of the constituencies of the city of Winnipeg. How much was paid during that period for unemployment insurance in each constituency?

Item agreed to.
597.	To reimburse the unemployment insurance fund under section 87F(1) of the Unemployment Insurance Act. 1940, as amended by statute of 1950, $1,780,000.

I notice that this item comes under section 87F (1) of the Unemployment Insurance Act. There were four new classes added by the amendment of last year. Has the minister figures to show

how much is for each class? What I particularly rose for was to speak about the operation of the unemployment assistance that we had in Newfoundland in the winter of 1949-50. Through inexperience I suppose as much as inadvertence, several hundred, I believe indeed thousands, of persons were not considered eligible for this unemployment assistance. Mistakes were made by the officials handling unemployment insurance for the first time. I was speaking to the manager down there, Mr. O'Grady, of the case of several workers who had 85 days in instead of 90 days. He admitted to me that it was possible to work now the other five days, on this new arrangement. That was done in several of the cases of the workmen, but one of the minor officials said it could not be done in the other case. I wonder if the minister knows now about that position? My first question was with regard to the proportion of this money which will be spent on the different classes.

I shall read the remarks of the hon. member for Cape Breton South as they appear in Hansard, and do what can be done.
The hon. member who has just taken his seat will recall that last year upon the amendment made to the Unemployment Insurance Act the supplementary payments were payable only from February 28 until April 15. Consequently it was quite a rush for the officials in all parts of Canada to get the new changes into the picture. I would imagine there may have been cases where some who felt they were entitled to supplementary benefits did not get them because of a lack of a clear understanding of the regulations. I have in my hand a document which shows that the amount of supplementary benefits paid in Newfoundland during that short period was $3,955.90. This amount was expended in the last fiscal year, and this item in the estimates is to reimburse the fund to the extent of $1,780,000.

Item agreed to.

I was under the impression that the Food and Drugs Act was still under the Department of National Revenue. Apparently however it has been transferred to the Department of National Health and Welfare.
There are three kinds of gin: there is gin; there is compound gin, and there is blended gin. I would ask the minister for the formula for each kind of gin.

577. To provide for payments to Trans-Canada Airlines of the difference in cost between air transportation and minimum tourist class ocean transportation for immigrants transported from the United Kingdom by Trans-Canada Airlines during the period of November 29, 1950, to March 31, 1951, $380,000.
May we have an explanation?

This is something that
members of the house know very little about?
That is why I wish to have an explanation.
Could the minister give us a brief explanation of what this means, what is being done, and how the money is being spent?

speakeroldname: Hon. W. E. Harris (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration):
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, in order to speed the movement of immigrants to Canada it was decided at December 1 that T.C.A. might be used to some extent. The plan evolved was that any immigrant starting from the United Kingdom, though not necessarily a person resident in the United Kingdom, might come by T.C.A., upon the payment of $160, which is the tourist passage by steamship, and that the remaining portion of the normal passage cost on T.C.A. would be met by the government. That works out to $215.50. There will be something like 1,750 of these persons between the period December 1 and March 31, at the end of the fiscal year.

Are those specially selected people? Are they technicians or specialists of any kind?

Supply-Citizenship and Immigration
We try to give priority to them. But a good deal of it depends upon the desire of the immigrant to come by that particular form of transportation.
How does the minister arrive at this amount?
The minister has explained with regard to the difference between the $160 and the T.C.A. fare paid under this item. I do not think he told us however who pays the $160.
The immigrant pays the $160.

Would the
minister take us into his confidence and tell us more about the plan? What happens to the people when they get the fare? Do they have to have a certain minimum of money when they arrive? There are several things of which I am ignorant and which it seems to me would be of interest to hon. members- unless, of course, others are better informed than I am. If not perhaps the minister would give some further information.

There is nothing unusual about this. It applies to any immigrant who can meet our requirements otherwise. I could discuss the requirements in connection with immigration when we are discussing other items, quite as well as in connection with this one. There are absolutely no strings attached, except that one who wishes to come by T.C.A. has to pay the $160. And of course such persons must have met all the other requirements of our immigration program.

Is this the
appropriate place to ask what arrangements if any there are for his housing when he arrives, and for his employment? If the minister would prefer to discuss the matter at some other time, I do not mind. However, it is a question which it seems to me is relevant.

Those matters
are relevant to all problems of immigration, of course. But anyone from the United Kingdom is entitled to come to Canada, if such person has met the health requirements and has some means whereby he will not be a public charge. He does not necessarily have to have assured employment, although in most cases he should have a sponsor for that purpose. I venture to say that ninety-nine per cent of these people are either persons coming to assured employment, or the dependents of persons already here.

How many did the minister say he anticipates will be here by March 31?
[Mr. Coldwell.)

About 1,750,
within a few one way or the other.

I am not very good at
arithmetic, but if one divides this $380,000 by $115, the amount the minister said the department had put up-
Oh, I did not hear the figure.
Are these all from the United Kingdom?

No. It applies
to anyone who is in the United Kingdom and who wishes to come forward by this means.
They must come to the United Kingdom first?
Yes.

Mr. Chairman, the real crux
of the problem of immigration has not been touched by hon. members who have asked these questions. The real crux of the problem is this: Do we need immigrants?
Yes.
One hon. member says yes.
I say yes, too.

It is a matter of opinion. When I went to London some years ago I met a gentleman who told be that Duchess So and So desired to see me. I was greatly impressed because that was the first time that such a thing had happened to me. I went to pay my respects to the beautiful duchess and she told me she had been in Canada and had found it a beautiful country, but there were not enough people there. I told her that if she decided to come to Canada again she would be one more charming person in our country. She smiled graciously.
Then I went back to where I was staying and another gentleman came to see me and told me another lady would like to see me. I told him I was pleased but I had just been to see a duchess and did not want to see anyone else. He told me that she was Marchioness So and So, and I told him I would go to see her. The marchioness asked me if I was a member of parliament and I told her I was. She told me that she thought Canada was a great country, that she understood its motto was, "From sea to sea," between two oceans. I told her in that way it was the same as England, only larger. She also thought that there was not enough population. She told me we needed more people in Canada.
That is the kind of propaganda that is used, flattery and fine words from attractive women. It did not go further. I am sure the hon.

member who suggested a minute ago that there should be more immigration has met many duchesses and marchionesses and countesses who think Canada is a great country but without enough people.
There are many unemployed in this country and I do not think they are all just day labourers. We are told that the immigrants who come here are technicians and specialists in trade and industry. If they are, well and good. But if they are coming here to take the place of Canadians in our hospitals or in our labour ranks, then I am opposed to it. I am making a clear distinction. There are some hon. members who are such imperialists that whenever a man or woman comes from any European country through Great Britain they consider it is something like the buildings that were marked with the blood of the lamb at the time of the Jews in the Old Testament-they are O.K., they have passed through the holy land of our time. That is not enough.
On the part of all men in the labour ranks who are not employed I protest against the bringing to Canada of anyone who is not a specialist in industry.
From where?

Anyone from anywhere who is a specialist in industry. I am not anti-British, I am pro-Canadian. I want to make that clear because there are some people who do not seem to understand it. They are ready to swallow anything under a British label. We must be Canadians first. I know that many people are unemployed and what has been said tonight about unemployment insurance confirms that fact. We are having to pay unemployment insurance benefits to Canadians and yet the doors are wide open for people to come in from outside to enjoy these benefits at the expense of the Canadian taxpayers.
I am not against immigration, but as I said in Westminster hall in London, Canada is not to be a dumping ground for all the nations in the world. We have to look after our own people first. We have unemployment insurance and it must be available to those who have been here long enough to qualify them for the payment of taxation that is paid by other Canadians.
We should welcome specialists in industry from all countries of the world, but we should not have to receive migratory birds who will be just passers-by with an ultimate destination in the United States or some South American country. I am in favour of bona fide immigrants, but I am not in favour of the other type. I ask the minister how many 80709-9U

How is it that no member of the opposition has given any information to the minister about the charges that have been laid against immigration officials in the old country or on the continent? Do they suffer from amnesia?

The hon. member has been
speaking most of the time.

The hon. member from
Kamloops is like all the other Tories. They are all ready to swallow anything, to swallow immigrants from all parts of the world who come here to take the place of Canadians who are unemployed.
Liberal policy.
Hon. members should remember that their leader hired planes to bring more Britishers to Ontario and I would refresh their memories in regard to that.
Good immigrants.
None better.

Where would you get
them?

Immigrants from Great
Britain, immigrants from Europe or the continent, immigrants from the United States if they find Canada to be a better country, immigrants from anywhere provided they are willing to be Canadians, provided that they are fit, provided that they are self-supporting.

We were
all immigrants originally.

They may come from anywhere. I know people from the Nordic countries and central Europe who are excellent Canadian citizens. I know of people from the British isles who are good Canadians. As I said before in the house, some of them are better than people who were born here. That is not new. I said it before.
Say it again.

If the hon. member does not
remember what I said a minute ago he is too hard to teach and I shall not repeat it. We hear speeches about the fundamental freedoms and the rights of men but when anyone expresses his own opinion in the house in the defence of Canadians by birth, or Canadians by adoption, it is taboo. It should not be said. Well, no Tory or anybody else will prevent me from saying what I sincerely believe it my duty to say in the House of Commons.

We like to hear you rant.
