Thank you. My hon. friends know that I have no rancour but I want to warn the government against the intrusion into this country of many people who will be a burden for the taxpayers within a short time.
Hear, hear.

Now that my hon. friends
agree with me I thank them, and I hope in the future they will always agree with me.

Are any of these fares
xecoverable or are they entirely subsidized .by the government?
The $160 is paid by the immigrant. The $215 is paid by the government and is not recoverable.

Mr. Chairman, the committee lias been given some information as to what seem to me to be the bare essentials that go Into the making up of this item. Certain questions have .been asked by the hon. member for Temiscouata concerning which I think the committee is entitled to an answer. I think there are answers to some of the questions he has asked, and it seems to me it is the duty of the minister to provide them.
I should like to make one or two observations about the item. As we have been told by the minister, it provides for assistance of this particular kind to immigrants during the four-month period commencing December 1 and ending on the 31st of this month. It is anticipated there will be approximately 1,700 to 1,750 immigrants who will be taking advantage of this subsidy towards the expense of their air transport.
We should be told how this fits into some scheme. This is more than a four-month scheme. When it was announced in December I think the country was given to understand this was the beginning of a scheme that was to be continuous. It seems to me that the committee has not yet been given information on some essential aspects of this matter. It is obvious that the 1,700 people are merely a fraction of those who will be coming to our shores as immigrants during this four-month period. One must naturally ask, how is it that certain immigrants are selected to have the benefit of this subsidy, some small fraction out of the total? What is the basis of selection? Is it simply those who wish to come by air, or is it rather those who have special aptitudes or skills that are in urgent demand in this country at the present time?
We have been given no information on that subject, and it seems to me it is highly essential information that the committee ought to have. If there are intending immigrants who have skills that are in urgent demand in this


country at the present time, is 1,700 the total of such or is 1,700 the total for whom in this four-month period transportation space is available? What is it that determines the number, 1,700 or 1,750 in the four-month period? How then does this plan relate to plans for the coming year? Surely there is something much more in the minds of the government than simply a limited appropriation now to meet the needs of a limited number of immigrants for a limited period. Surely we should have a more comprehensive statement from the government. We sit here and' have to prod and needle all the time to get little tidbits of information. It seems to me it is high time the government came out in the open and made a comprehensive statement on the subject.
That leads me to make an observation concerning the questions put to the minister by the hon. member for Temiscouata. One does not have to share all the views expressed by the hon. member for Temiscouata to appreciate the force of some of the questions he has asked. I am. quite sure the minister has the answers to some of the questions put by the hon. member for Temiscouata. I am another member of this house who would like to hear a statement from the minister as to the number of immigrants who have become charges, who have been found later .to have health defects that were not discerned at the time of entry, and how many of them have become charges on the unemployment insurance fund.
Let us have the information in order that we may determine whether the hon. member for Temiscouata is drawing sound or unsound inferences. I think the minister has the answers to these questions, and I urge him to give them to the house so that there may be some serious attempt to set at rest a lot of these questions that are raised from time to time as they have been tonight.

Mr. Chairman, I do not have at this moment any figures to indicate that any persons in hospitals- have been displaced by immigrants. There may be some. If there are complaints of that kind of course we will look into them. We do have these complaints made regularly. We investigate them, and we do not say that there is not an immigrant hired in the place of someone but in many cases it is found that the inference to be drawn from that very thing is not that the immigrant has displaced the person who has lost his employment. I did not think that the house would want to engage in a long discussion of immigration. We have provision made in the main estimates for a continuation of this policy. I thought

that when, the main estimates came before the house we could have an extended debate on the whole policy of immigration, and the experience that has been built up in the past year. I think we could then debate it under circumstances that would be more conducive to coming to good conclusions than on the supplementary estimates of two or three items which are the result of a new policy devised since the house last met, and for which money is being voted for the limited period covered by the supplementaries.

I do not wish to be querulous with reference to the statement of the minister, but I do say that the committee has not been given the information at the present time that it ought to have. After all we are not suggesting-

What do you
want?

-an extended debate on the question of immigration policy. We are asking for essential information with respect to the plan for which an appropriation is to be provided for a four-month period. I have asked certain questions and the minister has given no information with regard to them. Has the minister nothing to say about this particular plan? I was not suggesting that we enter into a debate on the whole policy of immigration. I think, however, that a house that is being called upon now to vote $380,000, a tidy sum, for a four-month period for a particular plan is entitled to a good deal of information. Therefore I come back to the questions which I asked before and which were in the main unanswered.
How does this tie in with the plan? What is it that has established the figure of 1,700 or 1,750? Is it a limitation of the number of those who are applying for emigration from the United Kingdom and who have aptitudes and skills that are in urgent demand in this country at the present time? Is it a limitation on air transport facilities? What is it that has fixed this number? Let us have some information about it.
May I ask the minister also to be a little more explicit in dealing with the questions thrown about by the hon. member for Temiscouata, who seemed to be throwing them at the opposition benches instead of in the proper direction, namely, at the minister. Why should the opposition be expected to answer for the shortcomings-and goodness knows they are plenty-of the immigration policy of the government? I suggest to the hon. member for Temiscouata that this is an example of the error into which habit can lead even an earnest member of the house. When you get into the habit of railing at
Supply-Citizenship and Immigration those who happen to be sitting on the opposition benches, you are led info the habit of directing to the opposition benches questions concerning government policy and the elaboration of government immigration plans for which we modestly profess our inability to answer for the government. But I do think the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration owes it to all members of this house, not only the hon. member for Temiscouata but all those of us who have been asked by the hon. member to provide him with answers, to provide the information and answer the questions.

I want to correct what has
been said for the hon. member for Eglinton. I never asked the opposition to give me any information about the immigration policy of the government. All 1 said was that they were completely silent on what I considered the essential matter in the immigration policy. I did not blame them for not answering me. I said I was very much surprised that they had not asked those questions on the basis of the immigration policy; that is all. Now I will excuse myself for having intervened at this point, because I see the minister is very anxious to answer the questions that have been put to him by myself and rebroadcast by the hon. member for Eglinton.

I should like to say a few words on this very important matter, and at the outset of- my remarks I think I can say I concur to a certain extent in the words that have been uttered by the hon. member for Temiscouata. As he is against immigration unlimited, so I always will be opposed to immigration unlimited. I do not say that the plan mentioned by the minister is what we may call immigration unlimited; but while I am -not qualified to give the minister advice or warnings or anything like that, I can utter what is in mind on this special question, as I have always desired to do every time it has come before the house.
I should like to know, of those who have been coming and those who are to -come under this special arrangement how many technicians there were or will be, how many day labourers, how many farmers and so on. That would be very interesting to know, because as everyone is aware the percentage of population as between the cities and rural districts of Canada is increasing every day in favour of the cities. That situation should not exist, and certainly it should not be allowed to increase. Then I should like the minister to say whether under this scheme the screening of these immigrants will be as
1418	HOUSE OF
Supply-Citizenship and Immigration severe as the screening I called for the last time I took the floor on our immigration policy.
The hon. member for Temiscouata says no one has ever touched the main point of the immigration policy. There was an immigration policy which I believe is still the policy of the present minister; that is, that Canada must not receive more immigrants than she can absorb. This is the main point to be made on this question of immigration. If Canada cannot absorb more than let us say
75,000	or 100,000 a year, we should not bring in more than that number. There is one feature of this scheme I do not like very much, because I am afraid it might develop into some kind of a trade. I believe the minister stated that these immigrants will leave the United Kingdom by plane. That is O.K., but let us say a few thousand come from other countries on the continent. They cross to the United Kingdom to comply with this scheme. It could develop into some kind of a trade, which would not be desirable because it would make the screening that much harder.
I believe we cannot talk too often and too firmly on this question of the screening of immigrants, not only in relation to physical health but in relation to mental health, intellectual and moral health, and political health. I believe those requirements are not too hard to comply with, but in any case I feel they are absolutely necessary especially in this period in which we are living. I have great confidence in the minister. Last year he told me the screening was to be very severe, and I hope he will not forget that this screening should cover the various issues I have mentioned, especially moral and political health.
Sometimes, even in the rural districts, we hear criticism which appears to be well founded. Some say these immigrants, not all but a few or perhaps many, come here with the assurance that they will have jobs. They even leave the United Kingdom or some other country of Europe with the assurance that their jobs are here waiting for them. That is a criticism we hear very often. Another is that we have a very real problem of housing in this country. I have been told by people in Montreal that some immigrants even have houses ready for them here. I was told of two instances in which friends of mine wanted to buy houses built under a certain housing scheme, only to be told that those houses were being kept, or had even been sold to some company, for the use of immigrants. That is another criticism I should like the minister to deal with, if not on this item then on the general item in the estimates having to do with immigration.

As I said a moment ago, I would be pleased to do that. I think we could debate immigration policy much better on the main estimates than on this item; but with respect to the questions asked by the hon. member for Eglinton, as I understand it he wants to know why this was done, why it is apparently limited to 1,750, and the basis of selection of those 1,750.
It was done because one of the problems we had to face in immigration was the lack of transportation. T.C.A. is flying certain regular flights from the United Kingdom here. It seemed logical, if there was space on T.C.A., that we should take advantage of that space. The numbers who are coming forward are the numbers that can be provided with transportation on the regular flights for immigrants in seats that are not taken up by other types of passengers.
As a matter of interest, the plan was announced on December 1, and because it took some time for arrangements to be made, and because of the Christmas season, there were not many who wished to come forward at that time. There were 79 in December; in January 461; in February 577, and the first two days of March, 48, making a total of 1,165. We have estimated that there will be 1,750 by the end of March. As I said before, there is an item in the main estimates continuing this plan. We believe that as long as there is available space we could use it in this operation. Have I covered all the questions?

Would the minister just confirm one inference I have drawn from his remarks? That figure has been arrived at because of the limitation on space available by T.C.A.; that has been the factor that has established the number?
On the regular flights, yes.
Then, within the ceiling established by the limitation of space on regular flights on T.C.A., what has been the basis of selection of the 1,700 from what must have been a larger number of applicants?
It comes down to this, then, that up to the present time the entire number of applicants has been contained within the limitation of space available on T.C.A., and there has been no selection?

And the numbers who indicated a desire to come in the summer months rather than in the winter months. As I say, we have bookings after March 31 of persons who in January said they would like to come by air in May or April or some other month.
Then what has been done to make the plan known in the United Kingdom or elsewhere where this type of immigrant has been invited?

Mr. Chairman, there was a poster issued immediately by T.C.A. Shortly after, in connection with another item we have here providing for assisted passage, we put out posters on a limited scale. I should say that the transportation agencies found it most convenient to advertise the schemes themselves, and there is ample publicity now in the United Kingdom and elsewhere for this plan.

I quite agree with the member for Temiscouata that we should not dump a lot of people in this country unless they have employment. I take it that most of those people who are coming here have employment somewhere in Canada. Could the minister give by provinces the number of people who are coming in under this system?

Mr. Chairman, I want to make it clear that this is not a special scheme, but only provides additional transportation facilities for those seeking to come to Canada from Europe. The persons who come under this scheme are persons who are otherwise admissible and who would come by ordinary passage if it were not for this scheme.
They would come in the regular quotas?

We have no
quotas against any particular country. We have certain qualifications which were mentioned by the member for Portneuf. I could give the house the statistics for last year's immigration, which would be a good guide to what we would logically expect this year, but perhaps I would do it at a later time. The figures show that roughly 60 to 65 per cent of the immigrants indicated a desire to go to Quebec and Ontario, and the remainder to the maritimes and the west.

Will some of this amount of $380,000 be repayable? What I have in mind
Supply-Citizenship and Immigration is that I believe there are some assisted passages when an immigrant comes here for a special purpose, when the employer pays part of the $160 and the balance over a period of time. I was wondering if that is done by the Department of Immigration or is that a matter which is looked after by the Department of Labour? Does this item include any portion which is repayable?
No, Mr. Chairman, no part of this is repayable. The assisted passage item appears under loans and investments at the end.

I still have the feeling which the member for Eglinton expressed that we are still not getting this story except in bits and pieces. The minister has said this is not a special scheme but is part of a larger undertaking. I believe that is what the member for Eglinton had in mind. The member for Temiscouata made a particular suggestion which, so far as I know, has not been answered. It came to me as a surprise, but he suggested that the whole thing was unsound because of a substantial amount of unemployment. I have not heard that answered. It came to me as a surprise, but perhaps the minister can answer it.
Another thing one hears is that private organizations have immigration plans and are making their own attempts to get people in substantial numbers. Are those in any way integrated with the larger plan? From before Christmas I carry in my mind that we heard a number, not 1,700 or 17,000, but many tens of thousands, perhaps over 100,000 immigrants for this year. I cannot see why this is not the natural time for us to get a somewhat comprehensive outline as to what the plan is. It may be many weeks before we are on the main estimates concerning immigration, and surely plans must exist. Why is this not the natural time for us to hear about them? For some reason the minister does not want to give them out.

Mr. Chairman, there is a later item for the assisted passage scheme, and I am sure that is what my hon. friend has in mind. If the committee reaches that item I shall go into detail on it, but I can only repeat what I said a minute ago that this is merely one method of providing transportation which is vitally needed because there is a scarcity of transportation for immigrants coming to Canada.

The minister states that anyone who desires can come by air. I think that is what he said. Who determines whether an immigrant from the British isles comes by air or by boat? Is it entirely up to the immigrant?
1420	HOUSE OF
Supply-Citizenship and Immigration
It is entirely up to the immigrant.
Then, Mr. Chairman, are we bringing any immigrants from European countries by air?

T.C.A. only operates as far as the United Kingdom. If people come to the United Kingdom they can then use this plan if they can make arrangements with T.C.A.
Mr. Cold well: When the service is established to Paris, will Paris be a place of embarkation?
That is a matter of government policy and the decision will be announced in due course.

The minister said an immigrant can apply to T.C.A. I have cases of people in my riding who have sent transportation, or arranged for transportation with the Trans-Canada Air Lines, to bring immigrants from the United Kingdom to my riding. These people have had to pay the full fare. It happened within the last month or so. Has any arrangement been made to reimburse these people? The immigrants are coming here definitely to do a job as domestics. In most cases the domestic promised to pay half the fare and the employer the other half. Has any arrangement been made to reimburse them?
I shall look into the matter that my hon. friend has mentioned and see him privately about it.

Something should be done about it. The people who have arranged the fares do not know about the assisted passage arrangement. They go down to the Trans-Canada Air Lines office and say: I want this to go to such and such an immigrant. The passage is arranged as to when the person can leave the United Kingdom to come here and that is all there is to it. It costs them full fare.

I was hoping that the minister was not going to brush off the questions put by the hon. member for Temiscouata without a fuller answer than he has just given. I should like to hear the minister make a comment on the suggestion that immigration has caused unemployment. The minister ought to be prepared to make a statement on the remarks made just a few minutes ago by the hon. member for Portneuf. He raised the question as to the absorptive capacity of this country. What has the government to say about the absorptive capacity of the country at the present time? How does it relate to the government's plans for encouraging immigration? We heard the


statement last December about the new plans. A question has been raised about the absorptive capacity of the country. The government should be prepared to give us a statement. They must have some conception of what they consider the absorptive capacity of the country to be at the present time. I ask the minister, for the benefit of all hon. members of the house, to answer these two important questions by the hon. member for Temiscouata and the hon. member for Portneuf, in relation to the plan of which this item is to provide for a part.

On the question
of the capacity of absorption, I said to the minister that I was ready to wait until the main item having to do with the policy on immigration was before the committee. I did not ask for a declaration from the minister right now. I am ready to wait until the special item on immigration comes before the house.
It is before the house now.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
What is before the house now, Mr. Chairman, is a supplementary estimate to carry out the policy that was announced and approved by the house in the general estimates for the year 1950-51. All those who are coming by these amounts are immigrants who have been certified as admissible to Canada. There is not sufficient transportation for them all to get here by ship, and there were regular flights on the Trans-Canada Air Lines that were not taken up by the ordinary passengers at that season of the year, and it was thought that that would be a convenient way of hastening the transportation to Canada of persons who had been certified under the plan that was approved in the general estimates for the year 1950-51.
In the estimates for the year 1951-52 there are substantial sums for the whole of the services of the immigration department, and when they are being discussed I think the whole policy for the year 1951-52 should be discussed, but I do not think it is usual to discuss the policy for the coming year on a supplementary estimate to take care of the expenses incurred in the current year; and that is all that is provided for by the supplementary estimates. They are all persons who have been certified by the services established as admissible to Canada. They have not been able to get here by boat, and there were those empty seats, or there would have been those empty seats, on the Trans-Canada Air Lines. Trans-Canada Air Lines operates only between England or Scotland and Canada, and it was made known that those who wanted to come could be accommodated in that way when there were seats that had not been sold to the ordinary

passengers. They get notice that there are a certain number of seats available, and they have to be prepared to come on very short notice. They express some ultimate desire to come at a certain time. They are told, if there is space you can come at that time; but this will not provide for the 1951-52 program. That program will be up before the house in a general estimate, and there will be full opportunity to discuss it then.
I do not think anyone feels that there has been, up to the present time, any overtaxing of the absorptive capacity of the country with respect to immigrants who have come forward.

This is the first satisfactory
explanation that the committee has got about item 577 of these estimates.

Are there among those
who find their way to England and come by air any number of displaced persons? Will the minister tell us how these displaced persons are screened? Who does the screening?

I do not use the
phrase "displaced persons" but those who do, I think, refer to persons under the management of the international refugee organization. If that is what my hon. friend has in mind, they do not come forward in this manner. They come from Europe by ordinary transportation.
It would be much easier to follow the Prime Minister in the statement he has just made if this item were not directly related to what was put before the people of Canada last December as a new plan.
By whom and when?

By the government in an announcement of the plan that was made. It may have been another case of someone speaking for the government; but certainly it was put before the people of Canada in the way I now describe and the government, so far as I am aware, has made no attempt to correct or alter the statement. It was that a plan was being inaugurated to bring 150,000 immigrants to Canada, and a concerted effort was to be made to interest in coming to Canada artisans and persons having those skills that are in urgent demand at the present time; and that to facilitate early movement of such immigrants into Canada with their skills the government was going to assist air passages and take other means to help bring these people to Canada at a time when their skills were in urgent demand. That, it seems to me, is the reason, and a very proper reason, why some of us have been asking questions
Supply-Citizenship and Immigration tonight designed to elicit necessary information relating to this item, because this item certainly represents the first four months' instalment of the new plan if the new plan is what the people of Canada were given last December to understand it to be.

The hon. member for Eglinton has entirely misconceived the information that he thinks he has received. In December the government of the province of Ontario made some announcement about their plans, and that is what I think my hon. friend was referring to, and what I think the hon. member for Greenwood was referring to.
That is not what I was referring to.

We made no announcement whatever in December except the plan we are now debating which was to bring forward people by Trans-Canada Air Lines, and that took effect on the 1st of December. There was no other announcement made in that month except with respect to persons under P.C. 2115. Well, during January the minister made a speech in which he said that it was expected that 150,000 people might come to Canada during this year, if that is the matter that my hon. friend has in mind. It was at that point that we announced assisted passage, which may be debated under a subsequent item of the supplementaries.

The minister has shed some light on the subject. I should like to ask him, in view of the answer he has just given, if then it is a fact that there is no new plan, so far as the government is concerned, with respect to encouraging further immigration to Canada?

If my hon. friend will look at page 13 of the further supplementary estimates he will see there item 648, which has to do with an assisted passage scheme. That is the only scheme I think we have any purpose in debating at this point- when we come to it.
That is not an answer to my question. I do not want to take up the time of the house -

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Oh no!
No!

I can tell some hon. members that I do want to get on with the business of the house, and if they want to do so the best thing they can do is to encourage ministers to give direct and simple answers to questions.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
The hon. member is out of order.

Supply-Citizenship and Immigration

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Ask simple questions, then.
I do not think I could put a more simple question than the last one, and it has not been answered yet.
What was that?
I will put the same question, to which I wish to have a short answer, in keeping with the standard prescribed by the Minister of Finance.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: A high standard.
Am I to infer that there is no new plan with respect to immigration, so far as the government is concerned?
Of course not. I have said twice that there was one, and it is described in item 648, which we will come to shortly-if this is passed.
The answer is yes and no.
The answer is that you are out of order.

Mr. Chairman, the Prime Minister has not clarified things at all. He has referred to a statement made in the session last year, when the regular estimates were before the House of Commons. There was no statement at that time which would explain the item now before us.
The minister knows perfectly well that the item now before us relates to an announcement made some time subsequent to the regular session, when it was stated that the government planned or that the government intended to provide part of the cost of air passages. There was some suggestion that it would apply particularly during the off season, when there would be space available on the transatlantic planes.
Now, that is a new plan, since the session. It being a new plan, a plan related.to this particular item, then I say this is the time for hon. members to find out why they are being asked to vote $380,000. I know that the figure mentioned here, without any explanation, of $380,000, may seem a mere pittance to a good many members; but the fact remains that at a time like this members should be asking themselves why they are voting this amount.
The minister has given a number of explanations in regard to the procedure by which intending immigrants may avail themselves of the funds available. A plan for assisted passages is justified only if it is a plan that is going to mean some substantial movement of people. If it is going to affect only a few people, then it simply means that some people who happen to learn about it will get a cheaper passage than others get, and it does


not mean any really important part of a planned immigration to this country. And, having regard to the expense of maintaining immigration offices, and carrying out the ordinary duties related to immigration, there simply is no justification for a plan of this kind, unless it is a real plan, and one that will bring a substantial number of people to this country.
The minister has explained that this is an additional amount which would take care of a substantial part of the passage-ini fact, more than half of the passage, where an immigrant applies for transportation by air and succeeds in getting it. It is available not only to people living in the British isles but it is also available to anyone who wishes to come to Canada, gets as far as the British isles and then decides to come the rest of the distance by air.
One of the things the minister certainly should explain in this connection, at a time when we are being asked to vote an item for the first time relating to this plan, is this: By what device does the immigration branch determine whether the individual who has arrived in England and is coming here is in fact a prospective immigrant, or is just a tourist who finds that this would be a cheap way to get to Canada?
Do not let the minister suggest that that does not happen. I know it does happen- and under a very much more carefully arranged plan than this. After all, why would not a person avail himself of this, unless there were some process which actually determined how this money is to be allocated? What the committee should have is an explanation in detail of a plan of this kind. We should know what the process is, from the time a person makes application until the time he gets here. Do they go to some office and do they then qualify before an immigration official for this special allowance, or do they simply go to the T.C.A. office in London, explain they want to fly to Canada and, if they get their reservation, make application under this plan?

Mr. Chairman, I can well understand that the leader of the opposition has had some experience in this. It may be that the plan he had in mind did work in such a way that occasionally some took advantage of it as tourists. There is always the possibility that that would happen. But so far as I know now, we have not found that to happen in respect of the eleven hundred, odd, who have come forward.
The procedure is simple. The applicant arrives at the immigration office. He passes through all the processes of becoming an

immigrant. He is investigated1, as is any ordinary immigrant. If after that he is passed as an immigrant-not as a tourist-he then may obtain passage by T.C.A. under this plan. That is always provided, of course, that there are demands for his services in this country, and that he is in all probability urgently needed at this moment, or will be very shortly.

That, Mr. Chairman, does not explain the detail at all. May I tell the minister, in case he has any wrong impressions, that not a handful of people among close to 20,000 who came into Ontario by air, under a different device, came for any purpose other than as straight immigrants. Nevertheless we did find that there might have been fifteen or twenty who availed themselves of the opportunity to come to Canada on a cheap fare-at that time it was $170.
I am only pointing out that in a plan of this kind, if an assisted passage is justified, there must be some definite procedure which assures that the assisted passage is for the purpose of bringing immigrants with a definite objective and who are going to be useful citizens in this country.
Now, it seems to me we have not yet anything before us to indicate that the immigration branch has assured itself in any way, first, that these people are really going to be able to fit into satisfactory jobs and, secondly, that they really are people who are coming out here with the idea of settling down as citizens in this country. If the minister has any explanation of that, then I certainly have not been able to find it in what he has said.

Perhaps the
leader of the opposition would accept my assurance that that is the case. I can disclose to him all the files of the 1,160 who have come. But let him for the moment, I hope, take my assurance that we check this movement of people, having in mind that it is an assisted passage-we check very carefully-and having in mind the necessity of bringing forward persons of the class he has described.

Mr. Chairman, this item 577 is to provide for payments to Trans-Canada Air Lines of the difference in cost in air transportation and minimum tourist class [DOT]ocean transportation for immigrants transported from the United Kingdom by Trans-Canada Air Lines during the period November 29, 1950, to March 31, 1951. This is the 19th of March and in twelve days we will have reached March 31. Is this $380,000 going to the T.C.A. to pay for past transportation or is it to pay for future transportation?
Supply-Citizenship and Immigration

It is for the
transportation of the 1,165 who had come up to March 2, and of the roughly 600 more we expect to come between March 2 and March 31.

When the
minister was describing the requirements which are required in the case of people coming to Canada under this scheme he used the words, "provided that there is a demand for his services in this country." Will the minister state what means are taken by the authorities to satisfy themselves on that point?

If I understand the question correctly it relates to the destination of the immigrant. If the immigrant is coming to assured employment he will qualify under this if that employment is in something which is urgently required.

Does that
mean that he will have made his own private arrangement with some person for employment?
Yes and no. There may be a demand sent by an employer to our offices in London which is filled in this manner or, alternatively, he may have made his own arrangements.

Mr. Chairman, a very
widespread impression has been created throughout this country that the government has inaugurated some new plan or policy with respect to immigration into Canada. Statements have been made and if they do not reflect government policy then I think in the interests of a proper understanding of the situation the house and country should be told.
Last September two senior officials of the Department of Citizenship and Immigration, on the immigration side, when departing for Europe in connection with certain duties, were quoted in the newspapers as saying that the Canadian government aimed to step up the flow of immigrants to 150,000 or 175,000 a year. The two officials concerned were Mr. C. E. S. Smith, director of the immigration department, and his deputy, Mr. George A. Benoit. They were leaving for Europe with a view to concentrating their efforts, so the newspaper statement indicates, on Britain, France, Germany, Italy and Switzerland, and attaining that which had been described as the goal of the government in this stepped-up program.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext:
Would the hon.
member quote the newspaper?

It appeared in several papers.

Supply-Citizenship and Immigration
Globe and Mail?
The statement was issued on September 25 on the departure of these two officials for Europe.
What paper?

It appeared in a number of papers. I am informed that it was made in Montreal on their departure for Europe. Whether the minister intended it or not, the speech which he made in Winnipeg on January 19 of this year was interpreted by many people as confirming the statement attributed to these officials in the previous September. The minister is reported in a Canadian Press dispatch from Winnipeg of January 19 as saying:
Our Objective-
Note the word "objective."
-for this year, assuming that conditions remain the same, is in the neighbourhood of 150,000. Of this number it is expected that over 30,000 will come from the United Kingdom. The balance will come largely from western Europe and will include some refugees.
Later on in the same dispatch the minister is quoted as saying:
Immigration is of great importance to Canada today. Through a vigorous, yet carefully controlled immigration program lies the solution to meeting, in part at least, the problem of national defence, and any real ability to participate fully in united undertakings against aggression. I
I think the minister should indicate whether the two officials who were quoted in the statement I have referred to were speaking with authority and were making a statement that reflected government policy, and whether the government has committed itself to an objective, as the minister put it, in the neighbourhood of 150,000 immigrants this year as compared with only 74,000 in 1950. If the minister is not prepared to say that the statement attributed to those two officials reflects government policy, then why did he use the word "objective" in his Winnipeg speech as indicated in the dispatch I have referred to? At that time, I repeat, he said:
Our objective for this year, assuming that conditions remain the same, is in the neighbourhood of 150,000.

The quotation
from the officials that has been read is new to me, but since the figure is approximately that which I gave in Winnipeg I do not think that any explanation is needed. As my hon. friend has quoted, in Winnipeg I said that under present conditions we thought that perhaps 150,000 people would come to Canada. I went on to say, what my hon. friend did not quote, that we thought those people could be absorbed into the national economy.

I still come back to the
purpose of this discussion and that is to find out whether there is a government plan with reference to this objective. The minister has just said that he thinks that 150,000 people will come this year, but that is not what the minister said in Winnipeg. In Winnipeg he said:
Our objective for this year, assuming that conditions remain the same, is in the neighbourhood of 150,000.
To an intelligent Canadian the use of the word "objective" would imply that the government has set a goal for itself. That is quite different from saying in a casual way, "Well, we think 150,000 people will come this year as compared with 74,000 last year."

What was your objective when
you were married?

Those who are not prepared to take the discussion of an important problem seriously should find means of amusing themselves elsewhere. I want to say to the minister, and I say this in a friendly spirit, that what he has said now is not what he said at Winnipeg. What he has said now does not indicate an objective set by government policy. What he had said is very different from indicating an objective which would be a matter of deliberate, conscious government policy.
Do I understand correctly that the T.C.A. is used to bring immigrants whose fares are partly paid by the government only when T.C.A. planes would be coming back without paying passengers?
In these particular seasons.

What becomes of these particular immigrants after they land in Canada? Has the department anyone there to guide them to their destination? I ask the question because I was coming up on the train the other day from Saint John, New Brunswick, and there were a dozen immigrants on it. They were on a C.P.R. train and they all had C.N.R. tickets. The conductor was going to put them off. I told him he had better take the tickets. They were going through to Grand Falls. I should like to know who was at the port to guide these immigrants when they came here.

I am glad the hon. member drew my attention to this. I am sure that everybody in the maritimes has been at a port at one time or another when a ship came in with immigrants. If they have they will realize that we have a large staff of persons there to look after them, to see that they get on the right trains and arrive at their destinations.
Why were they given Canadian National tickets on a C.P.R. train?
I must say I cannot understand that but I will make inquiries.
Was it not a pool train?

Mr. Chairman, the immigration department during the war and since has certainly been neglected by the government either intentionally or because of the fact that they believe that Canada does not need any immigrants. My hon. friend who is now in charge as minister of the department has proven his outstanding ability in other matters in this house. If he is given the department to run without unnecessary and continuous restraint and restriction I believe he is far-sighted enough to realize what Canada needs in the way of immigrants. If he is restricted it will certainly not be through lack of ability and knowledge on his part because in his heart he knows what Canada needs so far as immigrants are concerned. He knows that this land has not been given to the present generation of Canadians. He knows that our forefathers came here to expand a profitable and rich gift from God.
So far as the government is concerned, in the last fifteen years absolutely no desire or ability to expand this great country and develop its natural resources has been displayed by any of the minister's predecessors. Whether or not that is the wish of the cabinet nobody knows. I want to say that it is up to the minister not only to make speeches in Winnipeg and have representatives of his department make statements to the press prior to departing for Europe. He must realize, and I know he does, the serious attitude of the citizens of Canada with respect to what is going to happen so far as immigration is concerned. Are we going to be told there are not sufficient boats to bring these people here? Are we going to have curtailment of expansion of our industries owing to lack of labour?
We know that we are preaching unity in the world. We know that our representatives in the United Nations are preaching brotherly love but it was only recently that we considered this country no longer at war with Germany. Some of the finest settlers in this country were men and women who came from Germany, people of whom we are proud, and we are exceedingly proud of their children and grandchildren. We have men from Yugoslavia and their descendants, men from Iceland. Citizens of Canada have every right to point to them with pride and call them citizens of Canada because they have earned that title. Yet we are continuing a
Supply-Citizenship and Immigration policy of a paltry 75,000 immigrants a year. Knowing the minister as we do we know that is not his plan, and we know that is not his wish. We know it is somebody else's wish, somebody else's planning in the typical manner in which this government has been planning immigration for at least the last twenty years.
Some of us fought against the Germans. We took pot shots at them and they took pot shots at us. Sometimes they hit and sometimes we hit but when they were taken prisoners there was not the slightest animosity towards them for having been good soldiers. Why should we bear them ill will for being Hitler-trained in the last war? We could almost do the same thing with our youth under certain conditions and with the same kind of training that produced the SS troops. We point to them as people who should almost never be associated with again. That is poppycock and nonsense. Give these people what we have got to give. Set an example for these people from all these European countries and bar none excepting those from Russia.
Bring them here and spend one-tenth of what we spend to educate every man and woman in this country, which is approximately $5,000. Give them a break, and it is a cheap investment at $500 per educated person over the age of twenty, able bodied, medically examined, whom we bring to the Dominion of Canada. Let them help us develop the country. On the day the house closed last June I was travelling to my home town of Collingwood on the train from Toronto to Allandale.
Looking for help.

You would not have been much good if I had asked you to do the job. You would have done more talking than work. Let us get on with the talking now and I will proceed. There was a Roumanian doctor on the train with his wife who was a Viennese. They had tabs on them indicating that they were D.P.'s. With them were a man and his wife from Yugoslavia marked "domestic". There was another man and his wife marked "domestic" from Poland. With my poor French and the doctor's good French I was able to carry on a conversation with him. He in turn carried on a conversation with the people from Yugoslavia and Poland. That was the latter part of June when this house closed. Two months later I received a letter from the doctor written in almost perfect English saying that this was a land of opportunity and a great country. He is now working as a doctor in the Gravenhurst sanatorium and his wife is helping around the institution. A month
1426	HOUSE OF
Supply-Citizenship and Immigration later, I received word from the man from Yugoslavia who is working in am hotel in a northern town with his wife. Two months later the Pole wrote and thanked me for the information I had given to new citizens. I had told them that if they played the game they were just as good as any other Canadian citizen from the day they landed here. We Canadians came from the same kind of stock, the stock that is in a man from any country who is willing to work be he from the British isles, Yugoslavia, Poland, Germany or any other European country. He comes, he brings the right kind of stock and if he is a willing worker he is willing to become a loyal citizen of Canada. We cannot monopolize this country. The world has its eyes on Canada, a country of fourteen million people.
Hear, hear.

I suggest to my hon. friend who keeps interrupting that the new immigrants will forgive him. They will understand him the same as I do. He will not make any more impression on them than he makes in the House of Commons. He will not prevent them from becoming good citizens.
I want to prolong your speech.

Maybe it would not hurt, but it is time some of us said something that this government will understand, and make an appeal for broadening immigration. It is time that a man with the ability of the present minister was permitted to do something to tell the world that Canada, not only by words but by deeds, intends to show itself in its true colours and to open its doors to the right kind of immigrants without any nonsensical strings on them. Hundreds of thousands of people in devastated, grief-stricken Europe would be very happy to travel in boats with the same equipment we used to transport our brave soldiers during both wars. There are women in those countries who would make wonderful Canadian citizens and be the mothers of the children of the future, also willing to travel in that type of accommodation. But our ships are now gathering barnacles in our harbours, with the crews laid off. We have the transportation-
And the water.

Please make your own speech later. We are not getting along very quickly, with your foolish interjections. Please behave yourself. I would1 hate to have you called to order, but it will have to be done soon because your interjections are simply nonsense. You make your speech; I will make mine.


We are asking these people to pay $500, $600 or $700; people who have gone through a dreadful ordeal, who will be under the handicap of not being able to speak our language, and that money must be in American or Canadian dollars. That is a fortune to them. It seems to me that a little sincere effort on the part of the minister and his department should make it possible for these people to be brought here with about $350 left of their $500, to keep the wolf from the door and worry from their minds for a few months after their arrival. In other words they should be able to get here by paying $150 instead of $500. We have been trying to tell the Chinese we are pretty good people. We have been telling them we do not bear any animosity, and that they should not believe Mr. Stalin when he puts his arm around them. The truth is that the Chinese has proven himself a good citizen. But he wants to bring his wife from Hong Kong, and there is no effort on the part of the government to help him. He has to pay $1,000 to bring the wife that he loves as dearly as we love our wives.
Hear, hear.

Well, the hon. member probably would not love anyone, but after all the Chinese is a human being. We tell him we are the broadminded, western people; but we also tell him it will cost him $1,000 to be reunited with his wife. He may have been a Canadian citizen for years; he may have contributed in his own way as much as most Canadians and far more than many who have been here for generations and who are too proud to work. You know whom I mean as well as I do. Let us be realistic about this immigration situation. Many members of the cabinet are right-thinking; many of the men in the Liberal ranks are businessmen, but even today there is no semblance of business practice in the department. I should like to believe the minister has a plan almost complete. Dear knows he had to start from scratch to get that department in any kind of workable condition. But if he has a plan that would appeal to Canadians let him announce it in this house; let him tell the country all about it. Do not bring these immigrants and displaced persons here piecemeal. The minister knows as well as I do that any businessman, given authority to go to Europe with good screening teams, could bring back numbers of carpenters, bricklayers, farmers and all the rest of it. We could load our boats with bricklayers, carpenters, masons, plasterers, barbers, cooks and all the others we need. There should be nothing difficult about that. But there is no sign of a concrete

immigration plan even today with the possibility of an all-out war facing us. How are we going to man our munition factories, when our Canadian boys will have to go into the ranks?

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Order. I have given the hon. member every possible chance, I think, to discuss this item, which relates to payments to Trans-Canada Air Lines to make up the difference in cost between air transportation and minimum tourist class ocean transportation for immigrants, and I would ask him to direct his remarks to the item under consideration.

Very well, Mr. Chairman; I have never tried to be objectionable at any time. In conclusion let me simply say that I pray the minister to enlighten this country on one of the most vital subjects confronting Canada today, affecting as it does our hopes for the future.

Item agreed to.
648. To authorize and provide for a special account in the consolidated revenue fund from which interest-free loans may be made to heads of families or single persons, whose services are urgently required in Canada, towards the cost of ocean transportation to Canada and rail transportation in Canada from port of entry to destination-including cost of meals en route-under conditions fixed from time to time by the governor in council; and to authorize the crediting to such special account of repayments by immigrants and the readvancing of such repayments, $3,000,000.

In view of the
previous discussion I am sure there will be a few questions and I should make an explanation. This is the item everyone seems to want to talk about, but they wanted to do it under the previous item. We announced a policy for the purpose of bringing to Canada single persons or the heads of families whose skills are urgently needed in Canada at the present time. That plan calls for the loan to that person of his passage money, except for the sum of $30 which he is expected to put up himself in the currency of his own country. The loan of the passage money will be repayable by arrangement with the immigrant and his employer by deduction from his wages monthly over a period of twelve months in some cases but in no case to exceed twenty-four months. We expect we will require the $3 million to be voted here so that by the time the money starts coming in again by way of repayment we will have expended approximately this amount.
The reason for this is that the cost of transportation has been one of the factors which have delayed immigration to Canada, as the hon. member for Simcoe North just said. At
Supply-Citizenship and Immigration the same time we have done what we could to provide transportation for these people, and if the committee will permit me I should like to give an explanation of the transportation facilities. More than 30 vessels will make scheduled stops at Canadian ports during 1951. Five of these vessels did not visit Canadian ports last year. They are the La Guardia, the Homeland, the Europa, the Stockholm, and the Stavengerfjord. Several others have increased the number of scheduled stops. For example, the Scythia will make six more visits to Canada than she did during 1950. The Neptunia and the Italia will each make five additional visits to Canada. The Washington will make four more visits than she did last year.

On item 648, Mr. Chairman, I
should like to say a few words in tribute to the minister and his department for the new immigration facilities which were recently opened at the port of Saint John. When the member for Simcoe North was describing the lack of evidence of an immigration plan a few moments ago, I could not help but feel that he should have accepted my invitation to come to the port of Saint John a few weeks ago. He would then have seen some really concrete evidence of an immigration plan, because this building was opened a few short months ago.
We were given a picture of a bright future for this immigration policy which would be carried on by the department under the leadership of the present minister. This building is most modern, and probably the best equipped immigration station in North America. The building was commenced in 1948 and opened last December. It is located on the dockside and is more than 130 feet by 330 feet. It is bright and airy, and has excellent hospital facilities. It has the latest in restaurant and cafeteria equipment, and the detention quarters are of a superior nature.
The member for Fraser Valley is making a few suggestions, but I would suggest that he hold back for private members' night, because I am sure that before this session is completed he will have every opportunity to exhaust himself on the pipe line bills. I should like to pay particular tribute to the immigration work that is being carried on in the port of Saint John by the splendid volunteer organizations who are meeting the new immigrants and adding that touch of welcome which cannot be given by the regular efficient employees of the department. I should like to mention the Salvation Army, the lay members of the Baptist church, the Presbyterian church, the British and Foreign Missionary society, the Canadian Red Cross,
1428	HOUSE OF COMMONS
Supply-Citizenship and Immigration the Catholic Women's League, and the Sisters of Service. The Canadian Red Cross is operating an excellent nursery which is staffed and equipped through voluntary effort and subscription. I am sure that the excellent work carried on by these voluntary organizations in welcoming these new immigrants to our country could be helped by other organizations throughout the country who may wish to lend a hand.

Mr. Chairman, when we were asking questions on the previous item, I understood that the minister rather preferred to have us wait for item 648. I thought that when we came to this item our questions would be answered. So far as I am concerned they have not been answered at all. I can add one or two more to give the minister a start.
We have heard a description of the fine set-up at Saint John, but I should like to know something more about it. How many are employed there? How many people came through that port of entry? Is it going to be operated during the summer? How is this $3 million to be used? How much is to be for each family or each unit? Is there any estimate as to how often the fund will revolve? How many can be brought out under this plan during the year, and what is the relationship of this figure, which I understand is still an accepted figure, more or less a basic figure, of 150,000? We are still in the dark about that.

Mr. Chairman, to answer the first question first, the personnel at the port of Saint John in the immigration building totals about 15 to 18. For the period when a ship comes in, there are a good many more on a temporary basis.
The second question, as I understood it, was how much money is to be loaned? A person who benefits from this scheme provides $30 in the currency of his own country, and the Canadian government will lend him the difference between $30 and the cost of his transportation to Canada, including his transportation to any point in Canada, which works out to about $40 on the average.
The minister must have in his mind an average amount of money to each person on that basis?
It works out to just about $200.
In the case of a family?

This applies only to single workers or to the head of a family.

In other words, it is working hands that are required here, and the members of the family do not receive the benefit of this loan.

I was very much interested in what the member for Saint John-Albert said.
I had the pleasure, of course, of seeing this splendid shed, and I have known something about it. I agree when he says it is one of the finest immigration sheds in Canada, and perhaps in North America. There is one thing the people are very much concerned about, especially those who are employed in the shed, and that is whether these splendid facilities would be used for only a few months during the winter, or whether ships would be brought into Saint John to use those facilities which cannot be excelled anywhere else in Canada the year round. Really, I believe it is a great loss of money if those sheds are not used during the summer, just as they are during the winter. I should like the minister to say whether there is any intention of using these splendid facilities at the port of Saint John during the summer months.
I believe it is the desire of the department to use all its facilities to the maximum efficiency.

One of my
questions has not been answered. It was, how many came through the port of Saint John? I might ask the minister if my arithmetic is correct. He says there would be about $200 each, so the maximum would be about 15,000 people that might be accommodated under this particular item?

The first question was the number who came in. In December, there were 1,533; in January 280; and in February, 1,625. The 15,000, the expected number who will benefit by this plan, will probably come in, in the course of the next three, four or five months. We have only an estimate to go on. Over 30,000 persons applied in the offices in the United Kingdom and western Europe in the months of January and February for immigrant status. We are processing these now, and I should imagine that a very large number of these will come forward under the assisted passage scheme.

Will the
minister say how this compares with figures of a year ago?

We had no
assisted passage scheme a year ago.

No, but
would you not have figures of the applicants of a year ago?

Only 13,000 came forward from the United Kingdom in the whole of last year, so that my hon. friend can see that in the two months of January and February we received twice as many applications as came forward during the whole of the year.

Just before my hon. friend
goes on, these are further supplementary estimates, 1950-51, for the fiscal year ending March 31, 1951. What has been said about item 577 was about an amount that has to be spent from now until March 31; but item 648 is entirely different, and I wonder why it was not put in the main estimates which were tabled not long ago, because this amount of $3 million is apparently not for the supplementary estimates of 1950-51, but for the main estimate of 1951-52, and it is for future payments, not four or five months only. I ask the minister why it was not in the main estimates of 1951-52?

The plan was
announced effective February 1, so that to the extent of two months it would have been included in these supplementaries in any event, but in order that it should be made clear that it was a continuing plan on a revolving fund basis, we put it in for the full amount that we expected to use while the plan was in operation.
Item agreed to.

578.	Administration-further amount required, $22,082.

Under this item I want to clarify something that has appeared in the press just recently. This item has to do with reserves and trusts. In the riding that I have the honour to represent, Lambton-Kent, there is probably the largest Indian reserve in Canada. It contains something over 40,000 acres. There are close to 1,000 Indians in my riding. Adjacent to the reserve is a shooting and hunting marsh that the Indians have had the rights to for many years. This has been under lease and was called the St. Anne's lease. It was leased by a Toronto firm mainly for several years, but the department decided that it should be advertised and leased to someone else. They called for public tenders.
My experience with the Indian branch has been that the officials of the Indian affairs branch are very zealous of the Indians' rights. Any time that I have talked to them they have claimed that their first consideration is the Indian. I was rather bothered and
19. 1951	1429
Supply-Citizenship and Immigration disturbed over an item that appeared in the papers a few days ago. As a matter of fact, it appeared in the Journal last Thursday night. It was in the Globe and Mail, and I clipped this little item from the Windsor Star last Thursday. I will read it:
Hunters ask lease probe.
A parliamentary investigation of the federal government's action in leasing St. Anne's island in lake St. Clair, near Wallaceburg, to a private sportsmen's club was asked today by the Ontario federation of anglers and hunters in a brief to the legislature's fish and game committee.
K. S. Clarke, federation president, said that the lease had been "slipped over" by the federal department of Indian Affairs to a "highly objectionable" private club, whose members are mostly from the United States. "The amount of game that is taken from the island is something that the police might well look into," he said. The province had offered to pay the same amount, but the lease had been granted to the private club "for purely political reasons."
As the representative of that riding I want to know why it was granted for political reasons, because if it was I have no knowledge of it in the least.

I probably would not have commented except for the conclusion of the quotation. The St. Anne's lease is a well known lease in southwestern Ontario, and as my hon. friend says, the only interest that this department has in it is to obtain the maximum return from these grounds for the Indian band who surrendered part of the island in the first place. It has been under lease for something over sixty years, I think. Last year, as a result of a lawsuit, this lease came to an end and we had to re-lease that portion of the island because that was the basis on which the Indian band council had surrendered it. We advertised the hunting privileges in the Toronto Star, the Toronto Globe and Mail, the Windsor Star, the Chatham News, the London Free Press, the Sarnia Canadian Observer and the Detroit Free Press during July and August of last year. We asked for tenders, and they were opened on August 30, 1950. At that time there were three bids in the tenders, and we accepted the highest tender. That happened to be a number of persons, some Canadians and some Americans. A suggestion has been made that we ignored certain representations which had been made by a sportsmen's association in southwestern Ontario, but we did not receive any firm undertaking or bid from either the Ontario federation of anglers and hunters, the Kent county sportsmen's association or any similar organization in the province of Ontario.
I may repeat, our only interest is on behalf of the Indians who in fact are the beneficiaries of the lease.
